items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Problem - Bank C24 - Radome Composites Accruals and Classification.md
items.statement_html: The owner of Radome Composites S.L., which makes radar domes for aircraft noses, says: "In December we delivered 20 domes to an airline that will pay in February, so they are not sales of this year. We received in November a 30,000 m.u. advance for domes to be delivered next March, so that is income of this year. The electricity of December will be paid in January, so it is a cost of next year. And the five-year bank loan is all a long-term debt, even the instalment due next June."

subquestions.label: a
subquestions.prompt_html: Correct the owner's four statements using the accrual principle and the classification of the balance sheet
subquestions.hint_html: Revenues are recorded when the sale is made, expenses when goods and services are received, whether paid or not [Slide 8]. Current items are settled within one year [Slides 14-16].
subquestions.checkpoint_html:
• December deliveries: revenue of this year; the amount owed is an account receivable (current asset).
  • November advance: not revenue yet; a liability (unearned revenue) until delivery in March.
  • December electricity: expense of this year; unpaid amount is a current liability.
  • Loan: the instalment due next June is a current liability; the rest is long-term.
subquestions.solution_html:
Owner's statementCorrectionBasis
December deliveries are not sales of this yearThey are revenue of this year: the sale was made in December. The amount owed is an account receivable, a current assetRevenues are recorded when the sale is made, paid or not [Slide 8]; current assets [Slide 14]
The November advance is income of this yearIt is not revenue yet: no domes have been delivered. It is a liability (unearned revenue) until MarchLiabilities include unearned revenues [Slide 13]
December electricity is a cost of next yearIt is an expense of this year: the service was received in December. The unpaid amount is a current liabilityExpenses are recorded when the services are received [Slide 8]
The whole loan is long-termThe instalment due next June is a current liability; only the instalments due after one year are long-termCurrent liabilities are paid within the coming year [Slide 16]

subquestions.label: b
subquestions.prompt_html: Explain why the income statement and the balance sheet need these rules
subquestions.hint_html: What does each statement report, and over what time [Slides 7, 12]?
subquestions.checkpoint_html:
• The income statement reports performance over a period: it must match the revenues and expenses of that period, not cash movements.
  • The balance sheet reports the financial position at a point in time: classifying by maturity shows liquidity.
subquestions.solution_html: The income statement reports the performance of the business over a specific period [Slide 7]: it must contain the revenues earned and the expenses incurred in that period, whatever happens to the cash, otherwise the profit of a year would depend on when customers happen to pay. The balance sheet reports the financial position at a particular point in time [Slide 12]: splitting assets and liabilities into current and non-current shows whether the company can meet the debts due within the year with the resources that become cash within the year.

items.statement_html:
The newly appointed financial director of LOGÍSTICA FRIGORÍFICA DEL LEVANTE S.L. (FRIGOLEV), a company located in the port area of Castellón and dedicated to the manufacturing of isothermal containers and cold-chain storage equipment for agricultural exporters, is working on the closing of its financial statements (balance sheet and Income Statement) as of 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018).

The company was originally incorporated on 1 January 2016 (01/01/2016) by four partners, with an initial contribution of each of 1.500 m.u. disbursed fully in cash at that time, and no further capital modifications took place until fiscal year 2018. Due to the sudden departure of the previous chief accountant, the financial director only has an incomplete balance of the company as of 31 December 2017 (31/12/2017), which is included below with certain missing figures marked as (?), along with the audit notes detailing the operations that have taken place during the period from 1 January 2018 (01/01/2018) to 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018):

I. On 31 December 2017 (31/12/2017), the company had as depreciable fixed assets only the industrial refrigeration chambers purchased on a certain date during 2016, which have a useful life of 10 years and are amortized linearly with a residual value of 10% of their acquisition cost. In addition, the balance sheet at 31 December 2017 (31/12/2017) reflected an industrial plot of land acquired in 2016 and financial shares of other companies acquired as a permanent investment.

II. During the year 2018, the company has sold 3.600 units of isothermal containers at a catalog price of 25 m.u. / unit (every month the same amount, 300 u.). The general payment condition agreed with the customers implies that this will occur 60 days after the sale. However, a very important agricultural cooperative (representing 25% of the physical units sold each month), which has bought an equal amount every month, has been given a discount of 8% on the catalog price of their purchases in exchange for paying strictly in cash in the same month of the sale.

III. At 31 December 2017 (31/12/2017) there was a stock (stock in stock) of 400 tons of insulating raw material valued at 2,00 m.u. / ton. On 1 April 2018 (01/04/2018), the company purchased 5.000 tons of raw material at a cost of 2,00 m.u. / ton. The payment condition agreed with the suppliers was 40% paid in cash on the date of purchase, 30% payable to 90 days, and the remaining 30% deferred until 1 February 2019 (01/02/2019). At 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018), after conducting the warehouse count, there remains a final stock (stock in stock) of 900 tons.

IV. During the first quarter of 2018, the unpaid taxes and the outstanding supplier balances from the previous year were paid in full. Regarding the customer debt outstanding from 31 December 2017 (31/12/2017), 75% was charged in cash during the first semester of 2018, except 200 m.u. from a customer who requested and was granted a deferral of payment until 15 March 2019 (15/03/2019), and 100 m.u. corresponding to a client declared definitively insolvent on 1 June 2018 (01/06/2018), which must be recorded as an unrecoverable bad debt loss for the period.

V. Fixed personnel expenses have been 2.200 m.u. / month (to which 600 m.u. / month must be added for Social Security) from 1 January 2018 (01/01/2018). To respond to seasonal peaks in container assembly, production staff also received variable wages that amounted in 2018 to 3.620 m.u. Fixed and variable wages are paid in the month in which they are produced, whereas Social Security contributions (starting from January 2018) are paid on the 15th day of the following month. General expenses and utilities (electricity, phone, insurance, etc.) amounted to 1.100 m.u. / month and are paid two months after being made.

VI. The company carried out a renting contract on 1 March 2018 (01/03/2018) (with a duration of 2 years) with a specialized company for electric warehouse forklifts, for a value of 350 m.u. monthly. The contract establishes a condition of payment to 90 days (payment at the end of each month).

VII. On 1 April 2018 (01/04/2018), the company made a capital increase by issuing 1.000 new shares of 2,00 m.u. nominal value each, fully disbursed in cash and with an issue premium of 50% over the nominal value. On the same date, 1 April 2018 (01/04/2018), it bought two refrigerated delivery vehicles that cost a total of 4.800 m.u., of which it paid 50% in cash, postponing the payment of the remainder in two equal installments: half on 1 October 2018 (01/10/2018) and the other half on 1 April 2019 (01/04/2019). These vehicles will be amortized linearly in 6 years with a total residual value of 480 m.u. Furthermore, on 1 October 2018 (01/10/2018), it bought a software license for cold-chain tracking for a value of 1.600 m.u., payable to 120 days, which is amortized linearly in 4 years with residual value zero.

VIII. The long-term bank loan appearing on the balance sheet at 31 December 2017 (31/12/2017) was granted on 1 January 2017 (01/01/2017) at an annual interest rate of 6%. Each 31 December, the company must pay the accrued annual interest calculated from the loan value at the beginning of each year, and starting on 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018) it must also return to the bank an annual principal amount of 500 m.u. until completing the repayment on 31 December 2021 (31/12/2021). Additionally, on 1 July 2018 (01/07/2018), the company obtained a new short-term bank credit of 1.500 m.u. at 8% annual interest, agreeing to return 50% of the principal each semester for the next year. Both the principal installment and the semiannual interest calculated on the amount actually due in that semester will be paid the day after the end of each semester (i.e., on 1 January 2019 (01/01/2019) and 1 July 2019 (01/07/2019)).

IX. The financial results of the company are declared at 23:59 hrs on 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018). The applicable corporation tax rate is 25% on the Profits obtained, which is settled by calendar year and will be paid to the Treasury on 20 January 2019 (20/01/2019) (counted in the balance at 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018) as "unpaid taxes"). From the net profit after taxes, the company first offsets in full the losses from previous years, and of the remaining net profit, it retains 60% as reserves and distributes the other 40% as dividends to the shareholders, which are paid in cash before carrying out the final balance at 24:00 on 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018).

Step 1. New sales of the cooperative

$$75 \times 0{,}90 = 67{,}5 \text{ u./month}, \qquad 67{,}5 \times 25 = 1.687{,}5 \text{ m.u./month}, \qquad 12 \times 1.687{,}5 = 20.250 \text{ m.u.}$$
$$\Delta\text{Revenue} = 20.250 - 20.700 = -450 \text{ m.u.} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{Revenue} = 87.750 \text{ m.u.}$$

Step 2. Raw material (hypothesis 4)

In the base case 4.500 tons were consumed for 3.600 units: $4.500 / 3.600 = 1{,}25$ t/unit $= 2{,}50$ m.u./unit. Selling $12 \times 7{,}5 = 90$ units fewer:

$$\Delta\text{Consumption} = -90 \times 2{,}50 = -225 \text{ m.u.} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{final stock} = 1.800 + 225 = 2.025 \text{ m.u.}$$

$$\text{Profit before taxes} = 24.000 - 450 + 225 = 23.775, \qquad \text{Tax} = 0{,}25 \times 23.775 = 5.943{,}75$$
$$\text{Net profit} = 23.775 - 5.943{,}75 = 17.831{,}25, \qquad \text{Remaining} = 17.431{,}25$$
$$\text{Reserves} = 0{,}60 \times 17.431{,}25 = 10.458{,}75, \qquad \text{Dividends} = 0{,}40 \times 17.431{,}25 = 6.972{,}50$$

Step 4. New cash

The cooperative now pays at 60 days: January to October collected, $10 \times 1.687{,}5 = 16.875$ instead of 20.700 (−3.825). The dividend paid falls by 67,50; the tax is not paid in 2018.

$$\text{Cash} = 14.060 - 3.825 + 67{,}50 = 10.302{,}50 \text{ m.u.}$$

The profit is higher with the discount (18.000 against 17.831,25): removing the discount gains $2$ m.u. on each of the 810 units the cooperative still buys ($810 \times 2 = 1.620$ m.u.), but the 90 units it stops buying carried a margin over raw material of $23 - 2{,}50 = 20{,}50$ m.u. each ($90 \times 20{,}50 = 1.845$ m.u.); the net effect before taxes is $1.620 - 1.845 = -225$ m.u. items.statement_html:
The company AGRODRON LEVANTE S.L. was incorporated on 1 January 2017 (01/01/2017) by a group of agricultural engineers with a registered paid-in capital of 4.500 m.u., having an objective of providing precision crop-monitoring services by drone and distributing organic fertilizers in the region of Murcia.

The following information applies to fiscal year 2017:

To finance the operations of the company, on 1 January 2017 (01/01/2017) a bank granted the company a loan of 1.500 m.u. at 6% annual interest, with a duration of 5 years, i.e. until 31 December 2021 (31/12/2021). Each 31 December, the company must return to the bank an equal principal amount of 300 m.u. and should also pay the due annual interest (6%) calculated from the loan value at the beginning of each year.

During 2017, the company invested in a fleet of agricultural drones worth 2.400 m.u. The useful life of the drones purchased was 8 years (amortized linearly, with no residual value) and at the end of 2017 the company recorded in accumulated depreciation an amount of 75 m.u. for those assets. Also, a further investment of 400 m.u. in mapping software licenses was made on 31 December 2017 (31/12/2017) to process aerial images. They use these licenses for 4 years (linear amortization with residual value zero). In addition, the company spent 800 m.u. to purchase a plot of rural land for its flight testing base. Most of 2017 was devoted to obtaining civil aviation permits and only the actual business work was started in the final months of the year. At 31 December 2017 (31/12/2017), its balance sheet reflected a loss of 220 m.u., there was no stock (stock in stock) nor pending customer or supplier balances, and the cash in hand and bank account was 1.955 m.u.

The following information applies to fiscal year 2018:

  • For aerial crop monitoring, the average number of subscribed farms during 2018 was 400 with an average revenue of 0,45 m.u. / month per client in subscription fees. Additionally, the company billed 840 m.u. for the direct sales of organic fertilizers. At the end of 2018, AGRODRON had accounts receivable of 310 m.u. from their customers.
  • The company purchased supplies of organic fertilizers during 2018 which amounted to 500 m.u. Of these purchases, 70% was paid immediately in cash and the payment of the remaining 30% was deferred to the following year. Year 2018 sales consumed 80% of the purchased goods.
  • AGRODRON operates from rented hangars that have a monthly cost (from 1 January 2018 (01/01/2018)) of 25 m.u. / month, paid in cash. Fixed salaries and Social Security costs (contribution of the company to the Social Security) of the permanent employees amounted to 60 m.u. per month (from 1 January 2018 (01/01/2018)) and were paid in full in 2018. To respond to increased demand during the harvest campaign, the company hired external pilots whose variable wages amounted in 2018 to 192 m.u. (paid in cash).
  • Electricity, insurance, and other administrative expenditures totaled 180 m.u. in 2018. The company postponed the payment of 40% of this amount to the following year. Furthermore, on 1 July 2018 (01/07/2018), the company acquired thermal cameras for its drones for a value of 200 m.u., paying 50% in cash on that date and leaving the remainder payable to 9 months, i.e. on 1 April 2019 (01/04/2019). This equipment has a useful life of 5 years and will be amortized linearly with a residual value of 20%.
  • The financial results of the company are declared at 23:59 hrs on 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018). The applicable corporation tax rate was 25% on the Profits obtained and is payable in the first quarter of 2019. In 2018, the results were positive: after offsetting in full the loss of the previous year, the company decided to distribute 30% of the remaining net profit after taxes as dividends (paid at 24:00 on 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018)) and retain the rest in the company.

Required:

  1. Construct the Income Statement (Profit and Loss Account) of AGRODRON LEVANTE S.L. for the period ending 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018), and deduce the exact date in 2017 on which the fleet of agricultural drones was acquired.
  2. Construct and justify the balance sheet at 24:00 on 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018), detailing all intermediate cash and accrual calculations.
  3. Determine the values of the ROA and ROE ratios in 2018.
  4. Indicate which items of the balance sheet at 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018) would be affected and the exact amount of the effect if the decision was made before the end of 2018 to distribute the same dividend, but to pay it on 30 June 2019 (30/06/2019), and assuming simultaneously that the company had decided not to offset the loss of 2017 before calculating the 30% dividend payout.

The external auditor of TALLERES AERONÁUTICOS DEL HENARES S.A. (TAHSA), a company of Alcalá de Henares dedicated to the machining of titanium brackets and fittings for the aircraft structures industry, must issue the audit report on the financial statements (balance sheet and Income Statement) as of 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019). The auditor has the balance of the company as of 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018), which is included below, and the following operations that have taken place during the period from 1 January 2019 (01/01/2019) to 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019).

I. The company has sold during the year 2.400 brackets at a price of 8 m.u. / unit (every month the same amount, 200 u.). A part of the sales of each month, always the same percentage, is charged in cash in the moment of the sale; the rest is payable to 90 days. Unfortunately the commercial department has lost the contract that fixes this percentage.

II. During the first quarter of 2019, the unpaid taxes and the outstanding supplier balances of the previous year were paid. The customer debt outstanding from the previous year was charged in January, except 160 m.u. from an airline component maker declared in insolvency on 1 March 2019 (01/03/2019), which is definitively lost.

III. At 31 December 2018 (31/12/2018) there is a stock (stock in stock) of 800 kg of titanium bar valued at 1,50 m.u. / kg. On 1 February 2019 (01/02/2019) the company purchased 3.000 kg at 1,50 m.u. / kg, 50% payable to 60 days and the other 50% deferred until 1 February 2020 (01/02/2020). On 1 August 2019 (01/08/2019) it purchased 2.000 kg more at the same price, payable to 120 days. The count of 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019) shows 900 kg in the warehouse.

IV. Personnel expenses have been 400 m.u. / month (to which 120 m.u. / month must be added for Social Security); salaries are paid in the month in which they are produced and Social Security the month after. General expenses (electricity, insurance, cleaning) amount to 150 m.u. / month and are paid two months after being made.

V. The machinery of the balance of 2018 was bought on 1 January 2016 (01/01/2016) and is amortized linearly in 10 years with residual value zero. On 1 April 2019 (01/04/2019) the company bought a 5-axis CNC centre that cost 4.800 m.u., paid in full in cash that day. To finance it, the same day a bank granted a loan of 3.600 m.u. at 5% annual interest, to be returned in one single payment on 1 April 2022 (01/04/2022); the interest is paid every 1 April for the year that ends that day. The CNC centre will be amortized linearly in 8 years with a residual value of 480 m.u.

VI. The long-term loan of the balance of 2018 bears 4% annual interest. The company returns 300 m.u. of principal every 30 June and every 31 December, paying the same days the interest of the semester calculated on the debt at the beginning of the semester.

VII. On 1 October 2019 (01/10/2019) the shareholders subscribed a capital increase of 500 new shares of 2 m.u. nominal value, without issue premium, disbursing that day only 50%; the rest will be called in 2020. On 15 November 2019 (15/11/2019) the company received in cash a dividend of 80 m.u. from its financial shares in AEROPIEZAS S.A., a permanent investment.

items.statement_html:
AVIÓNICA DEL EBRO S.L. (AVIEBRO), a Zaragoza workshop dedicated to the repair and calibration of avionics equipment for regional airlines and flying schools, must present to the bank that finances it the financial statements (balance sheet and Income Statement) as of 30 June 2020 (30/06/2020). The financial director has the balance of 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019), included below, and the following operations of the first semester, from 1 January 2020 (01/01/2020) to 30 June 2020 (30/06/2020):

I. The company has invoiced repairs for 1.600 m.u. every month. The payment condition agreed with the customers is payable to 60 days. A regional airline, which represents 40% of the invoicing of every month, surpassed in March the annual volume agreed in its contract, and from 1 April 2020 (01/04/2020) it receives a discount of 5% on all its invoices.

II. The customer debt outstanding at 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019) was charged in January, except 250 m.u. from a flying school that has been granted to pay it on 30 September 2020 (30/09/2020). The suppliers of the previous year were paid in February. As the company closed 2019 with losses, there were no taxes to pay.

III. At 31 December 2019 (31/12/2019) there is a stock (stock in stock) of 300 spare parts valued at 2 m.u. / unit. On 1 February 2020 (01/02/2020) the company purchased 400 parts at 2 m.u., 50% paid in cash and 50% payable to 90 days; on 1 May 2020 (01/05/2020) it purchased 300 parts more at the same price, payable to 120 days. At 30 June 2020 (30/06/2020) there remain 250 parts in the warehouse.

IV. The technicians cost 600 m.u. / month, paid in the same month, to which 180 m.u. / month of Social Security must be added, paid the month after. The overheads (electricity, telephone, cleaning) are 100 m.u. / month and are paid two months after being made. On 1 March 2020 (01/03/2020) the company carried out a renting contract for a test bench of 120 m.u. monthly, paid at the end of each month.

V. The patent of the balance (a calibration procedure) is amortized linearly in 5 years with residual value zero; the computer equipment was bought on 1 January 2019 (01/01/2019) and is amortized linearly in 3 years with residual value zero.

VI. On 1 April 2020 (01/04/2020) AVIEBRO bought a small hangar next to the airport: the building is valued at 2.000 m.u. and the land at 1.000 m.u. It paid 20% in cash and the rest with a mortgage loan at 4% annual interest, to be returned in installments of 120 m.u. every 1 October and every 1 April, the first one on 1 October 2020 (01/10/2020); the same days it pays the interest of the semester calculated on the debt at the beginning of the semester. The building is amortized linearly in 50 years with residual value zero.

VII. The long-term loan of the balance bears 5% annual interest, which is paid every 31 December, and it is returned in one single payment on 31 December 2022 (31/12/2022).

VIII. The corporation tax is 25%. The taxable base of the semester is the profit before taxes minus the losses from previous years still pending to offset, and the resulting tax will be paid on 20 July 2020 (20/07/2020) (counted in the balance as "taxes to pay"). No dividends are distributed at the half-year.

Time window: six months, 01/01/2020–30/06/2020. Depreciation and interest are prorated by months; expenses are recorded when incurred even if they are paid later [Slide 8].

Hypotheses:

  1. The airline's discount applies to the invoices of April, May and June only.
  2. "Payable to 90 days" from 1 February means payment on 1 May; "payable to 120 days" from 1 May means payment at the end of August, outside the semester.
  3. The losses from previous years are offset for tax purposes, but they stay in the balance sheet until the annual meeting distributes the profit of the year; the result of the semester is shown separately in equity.
  4. Land is not depreciated.

Extension (not defined in the course decks). $\text{ROA} = \text{Income from operations}/\text{Total assets}$ and $\text{ROE} = \text{Net profit}/\text{Owners equity}$, both for the semester and on the balance at 30/06/2020.

The chief financial officer (CFO) of COMPOSITES AEROESPACIALES DE ÁLAVA S.A. (CAESA), a company of Vitoria dedicated to the manufacturing of carbon-fibre fairings for helicopters, is closing the books of the year 2021. The balance of the company at 31 December 2020 (31/12/2020) is included below; the operations of the period from 1 January 2021 (01/01/2021) to 31 December 2021 (31/12/2021) have been the following:

I. The company has sold 1.200 fairings at a price of 30 m.u. / unit (every month the same amount, 100 u.). Of the sales of every month, 20% is charged in cash and the remaining 80% is payable to 60 days. The customer debt of the previous year was charged in January, and the suppliers and the unpaid taxes of the previous year were paid in January and in April respectively.

II. At 31 December 2020 (31/12/2020) there is a stock (stock in stock) of 500 kg of epoxy resin valued at 3 m.u. / kg. On 1 March 2021 (01/03/2021) the company purchased 4.000 kg at 3 m.u. / kg, paying 30% in cash and the remaining 70% in two equal parts, on 1 September 2021 (01/09/2021) and on 1 March 2022 (01/03/2022). At 31 December 2021 (31/12/2021) there remain 700 kg in the warehouse.

III. The fixed salaries are 1.000 m.u. / month, paid in the same month, to which 300 m.u. / month of Social Security must be added, paid the month after. Variable wages of the lamination staff amounted in 2021 to 1.200 m.u. (paid in cash). The external supplies (energy for the autoclaves) are 250 m.u. / month and are paid two months after being made.

IV. The autoclave of the balance was bought on 1 January 2018 (01/01/2018) and is amortized linearly in 10 years with a residual value of 1.000 m.u. On 1 July 2021 (01/07/2021) CAESA put into service a second autoclave of 6.000 m.u. (amortized linearly in 10 years with a residual value of 600 m.u.) together with a software license for the control of the curing cycles of 1.200 m.u. (amortized linearly in 3 years with residual value zero), both paid in full in cash that day.

V. items.statement_html:
HELIPUERTOS Y SERVICIOS DEL CANTÁBRICO S.L. (HESECA) operates one helicopter from Santander for charter flights, offshore inspections and maintenance of other operators' aircraft. A trainee of the accounting firm that keeps its books has prepared, instead of the financial statements, the following summary of the ledger accounts of 2022, from 1 January 2022 (01/01/2022) to 31 December 2022 (31/12/2022). The partner of the firm asks you to prepare the balance sheet and the Income Statement as of 31 December 2022 (31/12/2022).

Opening balances at 1 January 2022 (01/01/2022): Customers 3.000; Spare parts 1.000; Bank 2.000; Helicopter (cost) 24.000; Accumulated depreciation of the helicopter 4.500; Van (cost) 1.800; Accumulated depreciation of the van 300; Paid-in capital 18.000; Reserves 1.500; Suppliers 1.200; Unpaid taxes 800; Bank loan 5.500.

Customers account: opening balance 3.000; invoiced in 2022 for flights and maintenance 34.000; collected in 2022 31.000; on 1 September 2022 (01/09/2022) a balance of 400 m.u. from an operator declared in bankruptcy was written off as definitively unrecoverable.

Spare parts and suppliers accounts: on 1 March 2022 (01/03/2022) parts were purchased for 3.000 m.u., 50% paid in cash and the rest payable to 60 days; on 1 September 2022 (01/09/2022) parts were purchased for 3.000 m.u. more, 50% payable to 30 days and the other 50% deferred until 1 March 2023 (01/03/2023). The suppliers' balance of the previous year was paid in January. The physical count of 31 December 2022 (31/12/2022) values the stock (stock in stock) of parts at 1.400 m.u.

Expense accounts (all paid by bank unless indicated): fuel 4.800; salaries of pilots and mechanics 9.600; Social Security 3.000, of which the contribution of December (250) is paid in January 2023; hangar rent 200 m.u. / month; on 1 October 2022 (01/10/2022) the annual insurance premium of the helicopter, 1.200 m.u., covering from 1 October 2022 (01/10/2022) to 30 September 2023 (30/09/2023), was paid in full. The unpaid taxes of 2021 were paid in January.

Fixed assets: the helicopter is amortized linearly in 12 years with a residual value of 10% of its cost, and was bought on a date that the trainee could not find; the van was bought on 1 January 2021 (01/01/2021) and is amortized linearly in 6 years with residual value zero.

Financing: the bank loan was granted on 1 January 2020 (01/01/2020) for 7.500 m.u. at 6% annual interest; every 31 December the company returns 1.000 m.u. and pays the interest calculated on the debt at the beginning of the year. On 1 May 2022 (01/05/2022) a bank opened a credit line with a limit of 4.000 m.u.: HESECA drew 2.000 m.u. that day and 1.000 m.u. more on 1 September 2022 (01/09/2022); it pays 9% annual interest only on the amount drawn, every 31 July, 31 October and 31 January, for the three months then ended.

Closing: the results are declared at 23:59 hrs on 31 December 2022 (31/12/2022). The corporation tax is 30% and will be paid in July 2023 ("taxes to pay"). The partners decided on 31 December 2022 (31/12/2022) a dividend of 30% of the profit after taxes, to be paid on 15 March 2023 (15/03/2023); the rest goes to reserves.

Required:

  1. Deduce the exact date on which the helicopter was purchased, and construct the Income Statement (Profit and Loss Account) of HESECA for the year 2022.
  2. Calculate the bank balance at 31 December 2022 (31/12/2022) and construct the balance sheet at that date, justifying the classification of every item.
  3. Determine the values of the ROA and ROE ratios in 2022, and indicate the effect on the balance sheet if the dividend had been paid at 24:00 on 31 December 2022 (31/12/2022).
  4. The trainee had recorded the whole insurance premium of 1.200 m.u. as an expense of 2022. Indicate what changes this error would produce in the Income Statement, the distribution of the profit and the balance sheet, and explain which statement it distorts and why.

items.title: What the NPV adds up
items.statement_html: The NPV of a project is the sum of its net cash flows minus the initial outlay, with every flow counted at its nominal value whatever the year in which it arrives.
items.explanation_html: That sum is only the NPV at a discount rate of 0%. The NPV discounts each flow to year 0, $NPV = -A + \sum_t Q_t/(1+k)^t$, so a flow received later is worth less today.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F01 - Unit 3 Investment Selection Criteria.md

items.title: The rate that cancels the NPV
items.statement_html: The internal rate of return of a project is the discount rate at which its NPV is equal to zero.
items.explanation_html: This is the definition used in the key: the IRR is the rate that makes the NPV equal to 0, which is why a known IRR lets one solve for the initial outlay.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F01 - Unit 3 Investment Selection Criteria.md

items.title: Ranking two projects below the cost of capital
items.statement_html: Two mutually exclusive projects have IRRs of 9% and 7%, and the cost of capital is 9.5%. Under the IRR criterion the company should undertake the project with the 9% IRR, because it ranks first.
items.explanation_html: Ranking is not enough: a project is accepted only if its IRR exceeds the cost of capital. Both IRRs are below 9.5%, so both NPVs at 9.5% are negative and neither project is accepted.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F01 - Unit 3 Investment Selection Criteria.md

items.title: IRR above the discount rate
items.statement_html: A project with conventional cash flows (an outlay followed by positive flows) has an IRR of 10%. If it is valued at a discount rate of 7%, its NPV is positive.
items.explanation_html: The NPV of such a project falls as the rate rises and is zero at the IRR. At 7%, below the 10% IRR, it is therefore positive (IRR > k).
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F01 - Unit 3 Investment Selection Criteria.md

items.title: Flows after the recovery
items.statement_html: The payback period takes into account every cash flow of the project, including those received after the initial outlay has been recovered.
items.explanation_html: The payback is the time it takes to recover the initial investment, so it stops counting at that moment and ignores every later flow. Two projects with the same payback can differ greatly in what they return afterwards.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F01 - Unit 3 Investment Selection Criteria.md

items.title: Fisher's rate of one project
items.statement_html: Fisher's rate of a project is the discount rate at which the NPV of that project becomes zero.
items.explanation_html: That is the IRR. Fisher's rate belongs to a pair of projects: it is the discount rate at which the two NPVs are equal, and it marks where the preferred project changes.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F01 - Unit 3 Investment Selection Criteria.md

items.title: The weighted average cost of capital
items.statement_html: The capital cost of a company is the average of the cost of its equity and the cost of its liabilities, each weighted by its share in the financial structure.
items.explanation_html: Topic 3 defines $K_{WACC} = K_{EQ}\,E/(E+L) + K_L\,L/(E+L)$; the key of Exercise 8 uses this weighted cost as the cut-off rate for the IRR.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F01 - Unit 3 Investment Selection Criteria.md

items.title: Is equity free
items.statement_html: Equity has no cost for the company, because the company does not pay interest on the funds contributed by its owners.
items.explanation_html: Every financial resource has a cost: liabilities have an explicit cost and equity an implicit (opportunity) cost, which enters the weighted average cost of capital.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F01 - Unit 3 Investment Selection Criteria.md

items.title: Raising the discount rate
items.statement_html: For a project made of an initial outlay followed by positive cash flows, a higher discount rate gives a lower NPV.
items.explanation_html: Each positive flow is divided by $(1+k)^t$, which grows with $k$, while the outlay at year 0 is not discounted; the NPV therefore decreases as the rate rises.
items.source_html: 3_II_NPV_NPV IRR_solutions.pdf, Exercise 6 (b); Examples PDF, Exercise 5 (c), table of NPVs at 0% and 8%.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F01 - Unit 3 Investment Selection Criteria.md

items.title: Equal NPVs at a zero rate
items.statement_html: If two projects have the same NPV at a discount rate of 0% (the same sum of net cash flows minus the outlay), then 0% is a Fisher's rate of that pair.
items.explanation_html: Fisher's rate is the rate at which both NPVs are equal; at 0% both NPVs equal their undiscounted sums, which are the same, so $r = 0\%$ solves the equation.
items.source_html: Examples PDF, Exercise 5 (c), pair A–B ($x = 1$, FR = 0%), and Exercise 6 (c).
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F01 - Unit 3 Investment Selection Criteria.md

items.title: What a Gantt chart shows
items.statement_html: A Gantt chart is a bar chart that normally shows the dependency relationships between the activities of a project, which makes it the preferred tool for planning complex projects.
items.explanation_html: The Gantt chart shows the scheduled start and stop dates of each step, but it normally does not show the dependency relationships between activities and it is used for non-complex projects.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F02 - Unit 4 Production Systems Costs and Leverage.md

items.title: Flexibility and cost
items.statement_html: Flexibility and cost are two objectives of the production function that can contradict each other.
items.explanation_html: The four objectives (cost, quality, time of delivery and flexibility) can conflict, and flexibility - cost is one of the pairs named by the course: making many different products in small amounts loses the savings of standard, large-scale production.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F02 - Unit 4 Production Systems Costs and Leverage.md

items.title: Characteristics of rigid production
items.statement_html: Rigid (continuous) production is characterized by flexible volumes of production, highly qualified workers and equipment for general use.
items.explanation_html: Those are the characteristics of flexible or intermittent production. Rigid production has big volumes, standard products sold at a low price and is capital intensive.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F02 - Unit 4 Production Systems Costs and Leverage.md

items.title: Flexible versus rigid below the crossing volume
items.statement_html: Below the volume at which the total cost lines of the two systems cross, a flexible production system is cheaper than a rigid one, because the rigid system starts with higher fixed costs.
items.explanation_html: The rigid system's total cost starts higher (more fixed cost) and grows more slowly (less variable cost per unit), so at low volumes (zone A) the flexible system is cheaper and at high volumes (zone B) the rigid one is.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F02 - Unit 4 Production Systems Costs and Leverage.md

items.title: Bottlenecks in a product layout
items.statement_html: In a product layout the pace of the line is set by the slowest machine, and a problem in one machine affects the whole process.
items.explanation_html: Both are disadvantages of the product layout listed by the course: time is set by the slowest machine (bottlenecks must be avoided) and a failure of one machine stops the whole flow.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F02 - Unit 4 Production Systems Costs and Leverage.md

items.title: Inventories under Just in Time
items.statement_html: Just in Time production relies on large safety inventories of finished products so that every customer request can be served at once.
items.explanation_html: Just in Time is based on requests and eliminates inventories; production is pulled by the orders, not served from stock.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F02 - Unit 4 Production Systems Costs and Leverage.md

items.title: Labour productivity
items.statement_html: Labour productivity is a total productivity index, because labour is the main factor of production of most firms.
items.explanation_html: Labour productivity (goods and services divided by labour) relates the output to one factor only, so it is a partial productivity index; the total index divides by labour, capital, raw materials and energy together.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F02 - Unit 4 Production Systems Costs and Leverage.md

items.title: A higher price and the break-even point
items.statement_html: If the selling price rises while the fixed costs and the variable cost per unit stay the same, the break-even point falls.
items.explanation_html: $Q_0 = FC/(P - VC)$: a higher price raises the unit margin $m = P - VC$, and the same fixed costs are covered with fewer units.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F02 - Unit 4 Production Systems Costs and Leverage.md

items.title: Sensitivity just above the break-even point
items.statement_html: A firm that sells slightly more than its break-even volume sees its operating profit change by much more than 1% when its sales change by 1%.
items.explanation_html: $OL = Q/(Q - Q^*)$: when $Q$ is just above $Q^*$ the denominator is small, so the operating leverage is large and the effect on profit is more than proportional.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F02 - Unit 4 Production Systems Costs and Leverage.md

items.title: Margin of safety in monetary units
items.statement_html: The margin of safety in monetary units is the difference between the actual volume and the break-even volume multiplied by the selling price.
items.explanation_html: In monetary units the margin of safety is $(Q - Q^*)\,m$: the units above the break-even point multiplied by the unit margin, not by the price, because each extra unit adds only its margin to the profit.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F02 - Unit 4 Production Systems Costs and Leverage.md

items.title: Where segmentation, positioning and price belong
items.statement_html: Market segmentation and the positioning of the product are formulated within strategic marketing, whereas setting the price of the product is a decision of operative marketing.
items.explanation_html: Segmentation and positioning are the strategies formulated in the last phase of strategic marketing (the analysis system), while price is one of the 4 Ps that operative marketing (the action system) combines in the marketing mix.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F03 - Unit 5 Marketing Concepts Mix and Elasticity.md

items.title: One-way and two-way processes
items.statement_html: Marketing differs from the sale in that marketing is a one-way process in which the company places its goods and services in front of the customer.
items.explanation_html: The one-way process is the sale. Marketing is a two-way process: goods and services go to the customer, and information about what the customer wants comes back to the company.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F03 - Unit 5 Marketing Concepts Mix and Elasticity.md

items.title: A new version inside an existing line
items.statement_html: When an avionics firm adds a new model to one of its existing product lines, the extension (width) of its product range increases.
items.explanation_html: The extension, or width (breadth), of the range is the number of product lines, which does not change. A new model inside an existing line increases the depth of that line (products per line) and the length of the range (total number of products).
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F03 - Unit 5 Marketing Concepts Mix and Elasticity.md

items.title: Raising the price of a product with inelastic demand
items.statement_html: If the demand for a product is inelastic, a rise in its price increases the income of the firm that sells it.
items.explanation_html: With $\lvert E_d \rvert < 1$ a 1% price rise lowers the quantity demanded by less than 1%, so almost the same quantity is sold at a higher price and income $I = P \cdot Q$ rises.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F03 - Unit 5 Marketing Concepts Mix and Elasticity.md

items.title: Several segments, several marketing mixes
items.statement_html: A firm that targets two or more segments and develops a distinct product and a separate marketing mix for each of them follows a differentiated concentrated (niche) strategy.
items.explanation_html: That is the wide differentiated (multisegment) strategy. The differentiated concentrated (niche) strategy aims the product and the marketing message at a single, well-defined segment.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F03 - Unit 5 Marketing Concepts Mix and Elasticity.md

items.title: Who the wholesaler sells to
items.statement_html: A wholesaler is an intermediary that sells to other intermediaries or to organisational buyers, but not to final consumers.
items.explanation_html: This is the course's definition of the wholesaler; the intermediary that sells consumer goods to final consumers for their personal or household use is the retailer.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F03 - Unit 5 Marketing Concepts Mix and Elasticity.md

items.title: The sign of the price elasticity coefficient
items.statement_html: By the law of demand the coefficient of price elasticity of demand is negative, which is why its absolute value is used to classify the demand as elastic or inelastic.
items.explanation_html: Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions, so the ratio of their percentage changes is negative; the course classifies the demand with $\lvert E_d \rvert$ compared with 1.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F03 - Unit 5 Marketing Concepts Mix and Elasticity.md

items.title: Influencer campaigns and the product
items.statement_html: A campaign on social networks with technology influencers is one of the product attributes of a firm, because it builds the image of the product.
items.explanation_html: The campaign belongs to the promotion (communication) policy of the marketing mix. The psychosocial attributes of the product are brand, design, packaging and quality, together with attributes such as warranty and post-sale service.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F03 - Unit 5 Marketing Concepts Mix and Elasticity.md

items.title: A negative cross elasticity
items.statement_html: If the cross elasticity of demand between two goods is negative, the two goods are complementary.
items.explanation_html: Cross elasticity is negative for complementary goods (a fall in the price of one raises the consumption of both) and positive for substitute goods.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F03 - Unit 5 Marketing Concepts Mix and Elasticity.md

items.title: How agents and brokers are paid
items.statement_html: Merchandise agents and brokers take title to the products they distribute and earn their income from the margin between their buying and selling prices.
items.explanation_html: Agents and brokers bring buyers and sellers together without owning title to the products, and they are paid a commission for their services.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F03 - Unit 5 Marketing Concepts Mix and Elasticity.md

items.title: What management is
items.statement_html: Management is the process of setting and achieving goals through four basic functions, planning, organizing, leading and controlling, that use human, financial and material resources.
items.explanation_html: This is the course's definition of management, and the four managerial functions are exactly planning, organizing, leading and controlling.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F04 - Unit 6 Decisions Structures and Control.md

items.title: Innovative decisions
items.statement_html: An innovative decision is taken when the problem is known and well defined and the alternative solutions are planned in advance.
items.explanation_html: A known, well-defined problem with known alternatives calls for a routine (planned) decision. An innovative (not planned) decision faces an unusual and ambiguous problem with ambiguous, unplanned alternatives.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F04 - Unit 6 Decisions Structures and Control.md

items.title: Order of the decision-making process
items.statement_html: In the decision-making process, the manager chooses an alternative first and only then analyses the alternatives that were considered.
items.explanation_html: Analysing the alternatives is step 4 and choosing an alternative is step 5: the choice comes after the analysis, never before it.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F04 - Unit 6 Decisions Structures and Control.md

items.title: Conceptual skills along the hierarchy
items.statement_html: Conceptual skills, the ability to see the firm as a whole, weigh more in top management than in first-line supervision.
items.explanation_html: The share of conceptual skills grows as one moves up the management hierarchy, while technical skills weigh most in low management; interpersonal skills are needed at every level.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F04 - Unit 6 Decisions Structures and Control.md

items.title: Publishing a job offer
items.statement_html: When an avionics firm publishes a job offer on an engineering job board to attract applicants, it is carrying out the selection of personnel.
items.explanation_html: Attracting applicants is recruitment, a Human Resources activity that comes before selection; selection is the later step that chooses among the candidates already recruited.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F04 - Unit 6 Decisions Structures and Control.md

items.title: The key part of the division organization
items.statement_html: In a division organization the middle line is the key part of the structure, and each autonomous division is itself organized as a bureaucracy.
items.explanation_html: The divisions are autonomous, the middle line is the key part, top management coordinates their performance and outputs, and each division is a bureaucracy.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F04 - Unit 6 Decisions Structures and Control.md

items.title: Analysts who design processes
items.statement_html: The analysts who design the systems and processes of the firm belong to the technostructure, not to the support staff.
items.explanation_html: The technostructure is formed by the analysts who design systems and processes; the support staff is the part that lies outside the operating workflow.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F04 - Unit 6 Decisions Structures and Control.md

items.title: Decision-making in a machine bureaucracy
items.statement_html: A machine bureaucracy combines decentralized decision-making with few hierarchical layers and a wide span of control.
items.explanation_html: A machine bureaucracy has centralized decision-making and a highly elaborated administrative structure with many layers and a low span of control. Decentralization belongs to the professional bureaucracy and the adhocracy.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F04 - Unit 6 Decisions Structures and Control.md

items.title: The weekly shift roster
items.statement_html: Drawing up next week's shift roster of an engine-assembly line is a strategic decision that belongs to top management.
items.explanation_html: A weekly shift roster is an operational decision of low management (first-line supervisors). Top management takes the strategic, general decisions that affect the firm as a whole.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F04 - Unit 6 Decisions Structures and Control.md

items.title: What controlling involves
items.statement_html: Controlling involves establishing standards, measuring actual performance, identifying deviations and taking corrective action if required, which is why planning and controlling are inseparable.
items.explanation_html: These are the four activities of controlling in the course, and the standards it measures against come from planning, so the two functions cannot be separated.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F04 - Unit 6 Decisions Structures and Control.md

items.title: Creativity of an organization
items.statement_html: The creativity of an organization depends not only on the creativity of its individuals but also on the social processes and contextual factors that shape the way those individuals interact.
items.explanation_html: The course defines organizational creativity as a function of the creativity of the individuals and of the social processes and contextual factors that shape their interaction; it is not a simple sum, because structure, routines and incentives can thwart or amplify individual creativity.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F05 - Unit 7 Innovation Types and Technology Cycles.md

items.title: A minor change called radical
items.statement_html: A new coating that slightly extends the life of an existing turbine blade, without changing the blade or the engine, is a radical innovation, because it improves an aerospace product.
items.explanation_html: A relatively minor change to existing practices is an incremental innovation; a radical innovation is very new and different from prior solutions. Improving a product does not make an innovation radical: the size of the departure from prior solutions does.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F05 - Unit 7 Innovation Types and Technology Cycles.md

items.title: Same innovation, two firms
items.statement_html: The same innovation can be competence-enhancing for one firm and competence-destroying for another firm of the same industry.
items.explanation_html: Whether an innovation enhances or destroys competences depends on whose perspective is taken: it enhances the competences of a firm whose existing knowledge base it builds on, and destroys those of a firm whose competences it does not use or renders obsolete.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F05 - Unit 7 Innovation Types and Technology Cycles.md

items.title: A new display in the same panel
items.statement_html: Replacing the analogue altimeter of a light aircraft with a digital one that fits the same slot of the instrument panel, without changing how the other systems of the aircraft interact, is an architectural innovation.
items.explanation_html: A change to one component that does not significantly affect the overall configuration of the system is a component (modular) innovation. An architectural innovation changes the overall design of the system or the way its components interact with each other, which this change does not do.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F05 - Unit 7 Innovation Types and Technology Cycles.md

items.title: Where the S-curve is steepest
items.statement_html: On the S-curve of technology performance, performance improves fastest when the first units of effort are invested in a new technology, and then grows more and more slowly.
items.explanation_html: Plotted against effort, performance improves slowly at first, then quickly, and finally flattens as it approaches the limit of the technology. The steepest part is in the middle of the curve, not at its beginning.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F05 - Unit 7 Innovation Types and Technology Cycles.md

items.title: Effort near the limit
items.statement_html: When a technology reaches the flat upper part of its S-curve, additional effort brings only small improvements in performance, because the technology is approaching its limit.
items.explanation_html: The upper part of the S-curve flattens towards the dotted line of the limit of the technology drawn on the slide, so each additional unit of effort yields a smaller gain in performance.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F05 - Unit 7 Innovation Types and Technology Cycles.md

items.title: A new knowledge base
items.statement_html: A discontinuous technology fulfils a similar market need to the existing technology by building on an entirely new knowledge base, and at first its performance may be lower than that of the technology it later overtakes.
items.explanation_html: This is the course's definition of a discontinuous technology; the second S-curve of the slide may start below the first technology and later cross it and reach a higher performance.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F05 - Unit 7 Innovation Types and Technology Cycles.md

items.title: What the diffusion curve plots
items.statement_html: The S-curve of technology diffusion plots the performance of a technology against the effort invested in developing it.
items.explanation_html: Performance against effort is the S-curve of technology performance. The diffusion S-curve plots the cumulative share of adopters against time (2.5%, 16%, 50%, 84% and 100% at the boundaries of the adopter categories), because diffusion is the spread of a technology through a population.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F05 - Unit 7 Innovation Types and Technology Cycles.md

items.title: The two majorities
items.statement_html: The early majority and the late majority each account for about 34% of the adopters of a technology, so together they make up about two thirds of the market.
items.explanation_html: The bell-shaped curve of market share gives 34% to the early majority and 34% to the late majority, 68% in total; innovators (2.5%), early adopters (13.5%) and laggards (16%) make up the rest.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F05 - Unit 7 Innovation Types and Technology Cycles.md

items.title: How a design becomes dominant
items.statement_html: A design becomes dominant only when a regulator or standards body officially enforces it; learning effects and network externalities play no part in its selection.
items.explanation_html: A dominant design is a de facto standard: it dominates its product category (usually 50% or more of the market) even if it is not officially enforced. The course gives learning effects and network externalities (installed base and complementary goods) as the reasons why dominant designs are selected.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank F05 - Unit 7 Innovation Types and Technology Cycles.md

items.title: NPV of a two-year project
items.statement_html: A project requires an initial outlay of 120,000 € and generates net cash flows of 70,000 € in year 1 and 80,000 € in year 2. With a yearly discount rate of 5%, its NPV is:

distractors.a: This is the undiscounted sum $70{,}000 + 80{,}000 - 120{,}000$, the NPV at 0%; the flows were not discounted.
distractors.b: Both flows were divided by $1.05^2$: the year 1 flow was discounted twice instead of once.
distractors.d: The present value of the inflows is right, but the initial outlay of 120,000 € was not subtracted.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B01 - Unit 3 NPV IRR Payback and Cost of Capital.md

items.title: Largest outlay compatible with a given IRR
items.statement_html: A project is expected to generate 25,000 € at the end of each of the next three years, and its estimated IRR is 6%. The maximum amount that can be invested in it at year 0 is:

distractors.b: This is $3 \times 25{,}000$: the flows were added without discounting them at the IRR.
distractors.c: The whole 75,000 € was discounted one year, as if every flow arrived at the end of year 1.
distractors.d: The whole 75,000 € was discounted three years, as if every flow arrived at the end of year 3.

items.source_html: 3_II_NPV IRR.pdf, Exercise 4 and its key (same method with four flows of 30,000 € at 8%).

items.title: Weighted average cost of capital
items.statement_html: A company is financed 35% with equity, whose cost is estimated at 12%, and 65% with liabilities, whose average cost is 5%. Its capital cost $K_{WACC}$ is:

distractors.a: This is the simple average $(12\% + 5\%)/2$; the costs were not weighted by the financial structure.
distractors.b: The weights were swapped: $0.65 \times 12\% + 0.35 \times 5\%$ gives the equity cost the weight of the liabilities.
distractors.c: The two costs were added, $12\% + 5\%$, which is not an average of any kind.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B01 - Unit 3 NPV IRR Payback and Cost of Capital.md

items.title: Payback with uneven flows
items.statement_html: A project requires 90,000 € and generates 30,000 €, 40,000 € and 50,000 € in years 1, 2 and 3. Assuming that each flow arrives evenly during its year, its payback period is:
items.explanation_html: After two years $30{,}000 + 40{,}000 = 70{,}000$ € are recovered; the remaining $90{,}000 - 70{,}000 = 20{,}000$ € come from the 50,000 € of year 3 after $20{,}000/50{,}000 = 0.40$ years, so the payback is 2.40 years.

distractors.a: The outlay was divided by the average flow, $90{,}000/40{,}000$; the payback follows the cumulative flows year by year, not their average.
distractors.c: The missing 20,000 € were divided by the year 1 flow (30,000 €) instead of the flow of year 3, the year in which the recovery happens.
distractors.d: The recovery was rounded up to the end of year 3, ignoring that the flows arrive evenly during the year.

items.source_html: 3_II_NPV_NPV IRR_solutions.pdf, Exercise 5 (b) and Exercise 9 (a) (fraction of the year in which the outlay is recovered).

items.title: What Fisher's rate is
items.statement_html: Fisher's rate of two investment projects is:

options.label: a
options.html: The discount rate at which the NPV of each project is zero

options.label: b
options.html: The weighted average of the costs of equity and liabilities of the company

options.label: c
options.html: The discount rate at which both projects have the same NPV

options.label: d
options.html: The discount rate at which each project recovers its initial outlay

items.explanation_html: The key of Exercise 9 obtains Fisher's rate from $NPV_A = NPV_B$; it is the rate at which the NPV profiles of the two projects cross, so the preferred project changes there.

distractors.a: The rate that makes the NPV of one project zero is its IRR, a property of a single project, not of a pair.
distractors.b: This is the capital cost $K_{WACC}$ of Slide 37, a property of the company's financing, not of two projects.
distractors.d: The time in which a project recovers its outlay is the payback period, which is measured in years, not a discount rate.

items.title: Both IRRs below the cost of capital
items.statement_html: Two mutually exclusive projects have IRRs of 9.2% (project A) and 8.4% (project B). The company's cost of capital is 9.5%. Under the IRR criterion, the company should:

options.label: a
options.html: Undertake A, because it has the higher IRR

options.label: b
options.html: Undertake both, because both IRRs are positive

options.label: c
options.html: Undertake B, because its outlay is recovered with a lower rate

options.label: d
options.html: Reject both, because both IRRs are below the cost of capital

items.explanation_html: A project is accepted only when its IRR exceeds the cost of capital; here $9.2\% < 9.5\%$ and $8.4\% < 9.5\%$, so both NPVs at 9.5% are negative and neither project is undertaken, whatever their ranking.

distractors.a: Ranking A above B is correct, but ranking alone does not make A acceptable: its IRR is still below the 9.5% cut-off rate.
distractors.b: A positive IRR is not the acceptance condition; the IRR must exceed the cost of capital, and the projects are mutually exclusive anyway.
distractors.c: A lower IRR makes a project less attractive, not more: this inverts the meaning of the IRR.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B01 - Unit 3 NPV IRR Payback and Cost of Capital.md

items.title: Effect of a higher discount rate
items.statement_html: A project made of an initial outlay followed by positive flows has an IRR of 12% and has been valued at 6%. If the discount rate is raised to 9%, its NPV:

options.label: b
options.html: Increases, because the project earns more than 9%

options.label: c
options.html: Becomes negative, because the rate has risen

options.label: d
options.html: Does not change, because the IRR does not depend on the rate

items.explanation_html: The NPV of such a project falls as the rate rises, so it is lower at 9% than at 6%; since 9% is still below the 12% IRR, at which the NPV is zero, it remains positive. The key of Exercise 6 reasons the same way for rates of 7% and 9% with an IRR of 10%.

distractors.b: A higher rate divides every future flow by a larger factor $(1+k)^t$, so the NPV cannot increase.
distractors.c: The NPV becomes negative only when the rate exceeds the IRR (12%), not as soon as it rises.
distractors.d: The IRR itself does not change, but the NPV is evaluated at the discount rate and does change with it.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B01 - Unit 3 NPV IRR Payback and Cost of Capital.md

items.title: A false statement about payback
items.statement_html: Which one of the following statements about the payback period is FALSE:

options.label: a
options.html: It is the time it takes to recover the initial investment from the project's cash flows

options.label: b
options.html: Of two projects, the one with the shorter payback always has the higher NPV

options.label: c
options.html: It does not take into account the cash flows received after the outlay is recovered

options.label: d
options.html: A project accepted under a maximum payback of three years may have a negative NPV

items.explanation_html: Payback and NPV can rank projects differently. In Exercise 9 of the sheet project B has the shorter payback (about 11 months against 1 year and 9 months), yet above Fisher's rate of about 5% project A has the higher NPV.

distractors.a: True: this is the definition used in the key of Exercise 5 (b), so it is not the false statement asked for.
distractors.c: True: payback stops counting when the outlay is recovered, which is why it ignores later flows; not the false one.
distractors.d: True: in Exercise 5 project A has a payback of one year and an NPV of −90.91 € at 10%, so this statement is not false.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B01 - Unit 3 NPV IRR Payback and Cost of Capital.md

items.title: IRR ranking against NPV at the cost of capital
items.statement_html: Two mutually exclusive projects: A has an IRR of 14% and B an IRR of 11%; B has the larger NPV at 0%, and their Fisher's rate is 7%. The company uses the NPV criterion with a cost of capital of 5%. It should choose:

options.label: a
options.html: A, because it has the higher IRR

options.label: b
options.html: Neither, because the IRRs disagree with the NPV at 0%

options.label: d
options.html: B, because below the Fisher's rate B has the higher NPV

items.explanation_html: The two NPV profiles cross only at Fisher's rate (7%). At 0% B has the larger NPV, so B stays above A for every rate below 7%; at 5% the NPV criterion chooses B, even though A has the higher IRR.

distractors.a: The IRR ranking holds only above Fisher's rate; at 5% it disagrees with the NPV ranking, and the company decides by NPV.
distractors.b: A disagreement between rankings does not make the projects unacceptable: both IRRs exceed 5%, so both NPVs are positive.
distractors.c: The projects are mutually exclusive, so only one of them can be undertaken even if both are acceptable.

items.title: The cost of each financial resource
items.statement_html: In the capital cost of the company, equity has ... cost and liabilities have ... cost:
items.explanation_html: Slide 37 states that every financial resource has a cost: equity has an implicit (opportunity) cost and liabilities an explicit cost (the interest), and both enter the weighted average $K_{WACC}$.

distractors.b: Equity is not free: the owners give up other uses of their funds, which is its opportunity cost.
distractors.c: The two kinds of cost were swapped: interest on liabilities is the explicit one.
distractors.d: Liabilities do carry a cost (their interest), and equity's cost is not explicit but implicit.

items.title: Which cost is variable
items.statement_html: A machining shop makes titanium brackets for aircraft seats. Which of the following costs is a variable cost:

options.label: a
options.html: The annual lease of the workshop

options.label: b
options.html: The salary of the plant manager

options.label: c
options.html: The titanium bar consumed by each bracket

options.label: d
options.html: The depreciation of the CNC machines

items.explanation_html: A variable cost grows with the volume produced, so total cost is $TC = FC + VC\,Q$ with $VC$ per unit (Topic 4, Slide 37). The titanium consumed by each bracket is spent once per unit, so it is a variable cost; the other three are paid whatever the volume, as the rent and the fixed staff costs of Exercise 1 of the examples PDF.

distractors.a: The lease is paid in full whether the shop makes one bracket or ten thousand, so it is a fixed cost.
distractors.b: A manager's salary does not depend on the number of brackets produced; it is a fixed cost of the period.
distractors.d: The yearly depreciation of the machines is the same at any volume of output, so it belongs to the fixed costs.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B02 - Unit 4 Break-Even Point Leverage and Production.md

items.title: Break-even volume
items.statement_html: A maker of avionics cooling fans has fixed costs of 900,000 € per year, sells each fan at 250 € and has a variable cost of 175 € per fan. Its break-even point is:
items.explanation_html: The unit margin is $m = P - VC = 250 - 175 = 75$ € per fan, and the break-even point is $Q_0 = FC/m = 900{,}000/75 = 12{,}000$ units (Topic 4, Slide 37).

distractors.b: 3,600 units divides the fixed costs by the price, 900,000/250, forgetting that each unit must also pay its own variable cost.
distractors.c: 5,143 units divides the fixed costs by the variable cost per unit, 900,000/175, which has no economic meaning.
distractors.d: 2,118 units adds price and variable cost, 900,000/(250 + 175), instead of subtracting them to get the margin.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B02 - Unit 4 Break-Even Point Leverage and Production.md

items.title: Break-even point with a commercial discount
items.statement_html: A supplier of cabin LED strips has a list price of 80 € per unit and gives a 10% commercial discount on the list price to all its customers. Its variable cost is 54 € per unit and its fixed costs are 360,000 € per year. Its break-even point is:
items.explanation_html: Revenue is earned at the net price, $P = 0.90 \times 80 = 72$ € per unit, so $m = 72 - 54 = 18$ € and $Q_0 = 360{,}000/18 = 20{,}000$ units (Topic 4, Slide 37; the discount is handled as in Examples PDF, Exercise 1).

distractors.a: 13,846 units uses the list price, 360,000/(80 − 54), as if no customer received the discount.
distractors.b: 15,385 units applies the 10% discount to the margin, 360,000/(0.9 × 26), instead of to the price; the variable cost is not discounted.
distractors.c: 5,000 units divides the fixed costs by the net price, 360,000/72, and forgets to subtract the variable cost.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B02 - Unit 4 Break-Even Point Leverage and Production.md

items.title: Effect of a fall in sales
items.statement_html: A drone maker has an operating leverage of 4 at its current volume. If its sales fall by 5%, what happens to its operating profit:

options.label: c
options.html: It falls by 5%, the same as the sales

items.explanation_html: $OL = (\Delta\text{Profit}/\text{Profit})/(\Delta Q/Q)$, so the relative change of the profit is $OL \times \Delta Q/Q = 4 \times (-5\%) = -20\%$ (Topic 4, Slides 39 and 40: with OL = 3 a 10% fall in sales lowers profit by 30%).

distractors.a: 1.25% divides the change in sales by the leverage, inverting the ratio that defines the OL.
distractors.c: A change equal to that of sales would mean OL = 1, which ignores the effect of the fixed costs.
distractors.d: 4% reads the leverage itself as the change in profit, forgetting to multiply it by the 5% change in sales.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B02 - Unit 4 Break-Even Point Leverage and Production.md

items.title: Leverage from the break-even point
items.statement_html: A firm that makes oxygen masks for airliners has a break-even point of 30,000 units and sells 40,000 units. Its operating leverage is:
items.explanation_html: Since $FC = Q^*\,m$, the leverage depends only on the distance to the break-even point: $OL = Q/(Q - Q^*) = 40{,}000/(40{,}000 - 30{,}000) = 4$ (Topic 4, Slide 42). A 1% change in sales changes the operating profit by 4%.

distractors.a: 0.25 is $(Q - Q^*)/Q$, the inverse of the right ratio.
distractors.b: 1.33 is $Q/Q^*$, which divides by the break-even volume instead of by the distance to it.
distractors.d: 3.00 is $Q^*/(Q - Q^*)$, with the break-even volume in the numerator instead of the actual volume.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B02 - Unit 4 Break-Even Point Leverage and Production.md

items.title: Leverage of a firm in losses
items.statement_html: A firm sells fewer units than its break-even point ($Q < Q^*$). Which one of the following statements about its operating leverage is TRUE:

options.label: a
options.html: It is greater than 1, so profit reacts more than proportionally to sales

options.label: b
options.html: It lies between 0 and 1, because the firm is in losses

options.label: c
options.html: It equals 1, because the fixed costs are not covered

options.label: d
options.html: It is zero or negative, and below −1 it amplifies the effect of a change in sales

items.explanation_html: With $Q < Q^*$ the denominator of $OL = Q/(Q - Q^*)$ is negative, so $OL \le 0$; for $OL < -1$ the effect is more than proportional (amplifier) and for $-1 < OL < 0$ it is less than proportional (Topic 4, Slide 42).

distractors.a: OL greater than 1 is the case of a firm with profits ($Q > Q^*$), not of a firm in losses.
distractors.b: No volume gives an OL between 0 and 1: above the break-even point OL > 1 and below it OL ≤ 0.
distractors.c: OL = 1 would need zero fixed costs; at the break-even point itself the leverage is not even defined.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B02 - Unit 4 Break-Even Point Leverage and Production.md

items.title: Type of production system
items.statement_html: A company builds satellite ground stations. Each station is designed for one client, and machinery, materials and workers are brought to the site where it is built. Its type of production and plant layout are:

options.label: a
options.html: Project production with a fixed layout

options.label: b
options.html: Batch production with a functional layout

options.label: c
options.html: Mass production with a product layout

options.label: d
options.html: Continuous production with a product layout

items.explanation_html: Individualized products with qualified workers and difficult planning are the project type, and a product that stays in one place while resources are brought to it is the fixed layout (Topic 4, Slides 7, 23 and 26).

distractors.b: Batch production makes a variety of products in batches in a functional layout; it does not build a single one-off unit on site.
distractors.c: Mass production makes standard products for mass markets along a line, the opposite of a design for one client.
distractors.d: Continuous production (petrochemistry) is the high-volume end of the product-process matrix, with no individualized product.

items.title: Total productivity index
items.statement_html: In one month a workshop that repairs aircraft wheels produces services worth 540,000 €. It uses labour worth 120,000 €, capital worth 90,000 €, raw materials worth 150,000 € and energy worth 40,000 €. Its total productivity index is:
items.explanation_html: Total productivity divides goods and services by all the factors together: $540{,}000/(120{,}000 + 90{,}000 + 150{,}000 + 40{,}000) = 540{,}000/400{,}000 = 1.35$ (Topic 4, Slide 34).

distractors.a: 4.50 is 540,000/120,000, the labour productivity: a partial index, not the total one.
distractors.b: 0.74 is 400,000/540,000, inputs over outputs, the inverse of the index.
distractors.c: 2.57 divides only by labour and capital, 540,000/210,000, leaving out raw materials and energy.

items.title: Fixed costs and economic risk
items.statement_html: Two firms of the same sector sell the same number of units and earn the same operating profit, but firm A has higher fixed costs than firm B. Which one of the following is TRUE:

options.label: a
options.html: Both have the same operating leverage, because they earn the same profit

options.label: b
options.html: Firm A has the higher operating leverage and therefore the higher economic risk

options.label: c
options.html: Firm B has the higher operating leverage, because its variable costs are higher

options.label: d
options.html: Firm A has the lower economic risk, because its fixed costs do not change with sales

items.explanation_html: $OL = Q\,m/\text{Profit}$. With the same profit, $Q\,m = \text{Profit} + FC$ is larger for the firm with higher fixed costs, so firm A has the higher OL; the OL is an index of economic (operating) risk and, ceteris paribus, higher fixed costs give a higher OL (Topic 4, Slides 39 and 41).

distractors.a: Equal profits do not give equal leverage: the numerator $Q\,m$ also contains the fixed costs, which differ.
distractors.c: Higher variable costs mean a smaller margin and smaller $Q\,m$ for the same profit, so firm B has the lower OL.
distractors.d: Fixed costs that do not change with sales are exactly what makes profit more sensitive to sales, so A carries more risk, not less.
