Steps 3 to 6 are therefore option b.

distractors.a: The alternatives cannot be analysed before they have been considered (generated): step 3 comes before step 4.
distractors.c: Choosing before analysing inverts steps 4 and 5; the choice must rest on the analysis of the alternatives.
distractors.d: Gathering information is step 2 and evaluating the results is step 7, so this list skips the analysis and the implementation.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B04 - Unit 6 Roles Configurations and People.md

items.title: A known fault with a written procedure
items.statement_html: A hangar supervisor meets a hydraulic leak that is well known to the team, and the maintenance manual gives the approved repair. Which type of decision does the supervisor take?
items.explanation_html: The problem is known and well defined and the alternative solution is known in advance (the manual), which is the definition of a routine, planned decision.

distractors.a: An innovative decision faces an unusual, ambiguous problem with unplanned alternatives, which is not the case of a fault the manual already covers.
distractors.b: An adaptable decision lies between the two extremes, for a problem or alternatives only partly known; here both are fully known.
distractors.c: Strategic classifies a decision by management level (top management), not by the type of problem and alternatives, and a single repair is not a strategic matter.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B04 - Unit 6 Roles Configurations and People.md

items.title: Presenting the results to the press
items.statement_html: At an air show, the CEO of a satellite manufacturer explains the firm's yearly results and plans to journalists. Which managerial role of Mintzberg does the CEO play?
items.explanation_html: Transmitting information about the firm to people outside it is the spokesperson role, one of the three informational roles (monitor, disseminator, spokesperson). The slide lists the roles by name only; the meaning used here is the usual one of Mintzberg's classification.

distractors.b: The negotiator role means bargaining with another party (a supplier, a union); giving information to the press involves no negotiation.
distractors.c: The resource allocator decides how money, people and time are distributed inside the firm, which is not what a press briefing does.
distractors.d: The leader role concerns motivating and directing the firm's own employees, while here the audience is outside the firm.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B04 - Unit 6 Roles Configurations and People.md

items.title: Understanding how things operate
items.statement_html: Complete the sentence: "The ability to understand how things operate, which weighs most in low management, is the ______ skill."
items.explanation_html: The course defines the technical skill as the ability to understand how things operate; its share is largest for first-line supervisors and smallest for top management.

distractors.a: The conceptual skill is the ability to see the firm as a whole, and it weighs most in top management, not in low management.
distractors.b: The interpersonal skill is the ability to interact with people at work successfully, needed at every level of the hierarchy.
distractors.d: Decisional is a group of Mintzberg's managerial roles, not one of the three basic managerial skills.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B04 - Unit 6 Roles Configurations and People.md

items.title: The professional bureaucracy
items.statement_html: Which statement about the professional bureaucracy is false?

options.label: a
options.html: It relies on high horizontal specialization with highly qualified employees.

options.label: b
options.html: It coordinates through the standardization of outputs, skills and knowledge.

options.label: c
options.html: It concentrates decision-making power at the strategic apex.

options.label: d
options.html: It suits big organizations in a stable but complex environment.

items.explanation_html: The professional bureaucracy is decentralized: qualified professionals of the operating core decide on their own work, and the staff mainly supports that core. Centralized power belongs to the machine bureaucracy (and direct supervision by the apex to the simple structure).

distractors.a: This statement is true: high horizontal specialization with highly qualified employees is listed as a feature of the configuration.
distractors.b: This statement is true: standardization of outputs, skills and knowledge is how the professionals are coordinated.
distractors.d: This statement is true: the configuration is that of big organizations in a stable but complex environment.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B04 - Unit 6 Roles Configurations and People.md

items.title: Talking past the organization chart
items.statement_html: The organization chart of a drone maker says that problems between the design and the test departments go through the two department heads. In practice, the engineers of both departments solve them by talking directly at the coffee machine. What does this illustrate?

options.label: a
options.html: An informal structure, which together with the formal structure forms the real structure of the firm

options.label: b
options.html: A change of the formal structure, because management has redrawn the organization chart

options.label: c
options.html: Centralization of decision-making in the two department heads

options.label: d
options.html: The creation of a technostructure that designs new processes

items.explanation_html: Informal contacts, communications and ways of doing things that employees develop on their own are the informal structure; combined with the formal structure defined by management, they give the real structure.

distractors.b: The formal structure is defined by management, and in the case management has changed nothing: the chart still prescribes the old route.
distractors.c: The engineers bypass the heads, so decisions are taken lower down, which is the opposite of centralization.
distractors.d: The technostructure is a formal part made of analysts who design systems and processes, not a spontaneous habit of engineers.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B04 - Unit 6 Roles Configurations and People.md

items.title: A three-person CubeSat start-up
items.statement_html: A start-up of three people builds CubeSat components. The founder assigns and checks the work of the two engineers directly; there are no middle managers, analysts or support departments. Which basic configuration does it have?
items.explanation_html: Only a strategic apex (the founder) and an operating core (the engineers), coordination by direct supervision of the apex, and a start-up or very small business: these are the features of the simple structure.

distractors.a: An adhocracy mixes middle line, operating core and staff in a matrix of experts and is used as a complementary structure for specific projects; here there is no middle line or staff to mix.
distractors.b: A machine bureaucracy needs many rules, many hierarchical layers and a big, mature organization, the opposite of a three-person firm.
distractors.c: A division organization requires autonomous divisions led by a middle line, which a firm with no middle managers cannot have.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B04 - Unit 6 Roles Configurations and People.md

items.title: Recruitment and selection
items.statement_html: Complete the sentence: "Within human resources management, ______ attracts candidates to the firm and comes before ______, which chooses among them."
items.explanation_html: Human resources management is the process of recruiting, selecting, training, appraising and compensating employees, in that order. Recruitment attracts candidates and selection then chooses among them.

distractors.a: This inverts the two activities: selection cannot choose among candidates who have not yet been attracted by recruitment.
distractors.c: Training and performance appraisal act on people already hired, so neither attracts or chooses candidates.
distractors.d: Compensation rewards employees already in the firm, and recruitment comes first in the process, not after compensation.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B04 - Unit 6 Roles Configurations and People.md

items.title: The activities of controlling
items.statement_html: Which list gives the activities of controlling in the order of the course?

options.label: a
options.html: Establishing standards, measuring actual performance, identifying deviations, taking corrective action if required

options.label: b
options.html: Measuring actual performance, establishing standards, taking corrective action, identifying deviations

options.label: c
options.html: Developing forecasts, defining strategic objectives, developing alternative courses of action, deciding on a course of action

options.label: d
options.html: Recognizing the problem, gathering information, choosing an alternative, evaluating the results

items.explanation_html: Controlling ensures that activities provide the planned results: a standard is set first, actual performance is measured against it, deviations are identified and corrective action is taken if required.

distractors.b: Performance cannot be judged before a standard exists, and corrective action presupposes that a deviation has been identified first.
distractors.c: These are the four main steps of planning, the function that sets the goals controlling later checks.
distractors.d: These are steps of the decision-making process, not the activities of controlling.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B04 - Unit 6 Roles Configurations and People.md

items.title: Why an adhocracy for a prototype project
items.statement_html: An aircraft manufacturer sets up a team of designers, test engineers and suppliers' specialists to build an eVTOL demonstrator in eighteen months, organized as an adhocracy. Why does that configuration suit the project?

options.label: a
options.html: Because its high standardization and formalization reduce the errors of a new design

options.label: b
options.html: Because it concentrates every decision in the strategic apex, which speeds up approvals

options.label: c
options.html: Because its low standardization and formalization, decentralized decisions and matrix departmentalization give the flexibility an innovative project needs

options.label: d
options.html: Because its many hierarchical layers and low span of control keep a close check on each specialist

items.explanation_html: The adhocracy has high horizontal and low vertical specialization, low standardization and formalization, decentralization as the key to flexibility and matrix departmentalization, and it is used as a complementary structure for specific projects, which is the situation of the demonstrator.

distractors.a: High standardization and formalization describe the machine bureaucracy; in the adhocracy both are low and the technostructure disappears.
distractors.b: Centralization in the apex is the feature of the simple structure and of the machine bureaucracy; the adhocracy is decentralized.
distractors.d: Many layers and a low span of control are features of the machine bureaucracy, which would slow down an innovative project.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B04 - Unit 6 Roles Configurations and People.md

items.title: The most important source of innovation
items.statement_html: According to the course, which is the most important source of innovation:

options.label: a
options.html: The lone individual inventor working on a problem of his or her own

options.label: b
options.html: The linkages between individuals, firms, universities, government-funded research and private non-profit organizations

options.label: c
options.html: The central corporate research laboratories of large firms

options.label: d
options.html: Government laboratories, science parks and incubators

items.explanation_html: Topic 7, Slide 4: the most important source of innovation is the linkages between the players; networks of innovators that leverage knowledge and other resources from multiple sources are one of the most powerful agents of technological advance.

distractors.a: The individual inventor is one of the sources listed on Slide 3, but the course does not rank it first; it singles out the linkages between all the sources.
distractors.c: Central corporate research ranks first among firms' sources of research work on Slide 6, which is a ranking inside firms, not the most important source of innovation overall.
distractors.d: Government laboratories, science parks and incubators are one source among several (Slide 8), not the linkages that the course names as the most important source.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B05 - Unit 7 Sources of Innovation and Design Dominance.md

items.title: First source of development work
items.statement_html: In the ranking of the sources of development work reported by firms (Roberts, 2001), which source comes first:
items.explanation_html: Slide 6 gives two rankings. For development work the first source is internal R&D within divisions, followed by central corporate research and suppliers' technology.

distractors.a: Central corporate research is first for research work but second for development work; the option swaps the two rankings.
distractors.b: Suppliers' technology is third in the ranking of development work, behind the two internal sources of the firm.
distractors.c: Sponsored university research appears third in the ranking of research work and does not appear among the first sources of development work.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B05 - Unit 7 Sources of Innovation and Design Dominance.md

items.title: Knowledge that crosses boundaries
items.statement_html: A positive externality of R&D that results from the spread of knowledge across organizational or regional boundaries is called ...
items.explanation_html: Topic 7, Slide 9 defines technological spillovers as a positive externality of R&D resulting from the spread of knowledge across organizational or regional boundaries.

distractors.b: A technology cluster is a regional group of firms connected to a common technology, a set of firms, not the externality that flows between them.
distractors.c: Absorptive capacity is the ability of an organization to recognize, assimilate and use new knowledge (Slide 18), a capability of one firm, not a spread of knowledge.
distractors.d: A network externality is the rise in the value of a good to a user as the number of its users grows (Slide 19); it is not caused by spread R&D knowledge.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B05 - Unit 7 Sources of Innovation and Design Dominance.md

items.title: Robotic welding on the seat line
items.statement_html: An aircraft-seat manufacturer installs robotic welding on its assembly line. The defect rate of the seat frames halves and the number of seats produced per shift rises by 20%, while the seats delivered to airlines are identical to the previous ones. Which type of innovation is this:

options.label: a
options.html: A product innovation, because the seats are the firm's output

options.label: b
options.html: An architectural innovation, because the assembly line is a system

options.label: d
options.html: A dominant design of the seat industry

items.explanation_html: Process innovations change the way an organization conducts its business, such as the techniques of producing goods, and are often aimed at improving the effectiveness or efficiency of production by reducing defect rates or increasing the quantity produced in a given time, exactly what the robotic welding does (Slide 11).

distractors.a: A product innovation is embodied in the outputs; here the seats delivered are unchanged, so the novelty is not in the output.
distractors.b: Architectural innovation refers to a change in the overall design of a system and in how its components interact; nothing in the case changes the design of the seat or its configuration.
distractors.d: A dominant design is a product or process architecture that holds usually 50% or more of a market, not a single firm's improvement of its own line.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B05 - Unit 7 Sources of Innovation and Design Dominance.md

items.title: Competence-enhancing or destroying
items.statement_html: Which one of the following statements about competence-enhancing and competence-destroying innovations is FALSE:

options.label: a
options.html: Whether an innovation is competence-enhancing or competence-destroying depends on whose perspective is taken

options.label: b
options.html: A radical innovation is always competence-destroying for every firm of the industry

options.label: c
options.html: An innovation is competence-enhancing for a firm if it builds on that firm's existing knowledge base

options.label: d
options.html: An innovation is competence-destroying for a firm if it renders that firm's competencies obsolete

items.explanation_html: The statement is false because the course classifies competence effects firm by firm: the same innovation can enhance the competences of one firm and destroy those of another (Slide 12). Being radical (very new and different from prior solutions) is a different pair of the classification and does not fix the effect on every firm.

distractors.a: True: Slide 12 states that the classification depends on whose perspective is being taken.
distractors.c: True: this is the course's definition of competence-enhancing from the perspective of a particular firm.
distractors.d: True: this is the course's definition of competence-destroying, which also covers an innovation that does not build on the firm's competences.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B05 - Unit 7 Sources of Innovation and Design Dominance.md

items.title: From one rotor to four
items.statement_html: A drone maker moves from a single-rotor helicopter layout to a quadcopter. It keeps the same type of electric motors, batteries and cameras, but rearranges them and changes how they work together: the drone is now steered by varying the speed of four rotors instead of tilting the blades of one rotor. On the architectural vs component pair, this is ...

options.label: a
options.html: an architectural innovation, because it changes the overall design of the system and the way its components interact

options.label: b
options.html: a component innovation, because it changes one or more components without affecting the overall configuration

options.label: c
options.html: a component innovation, because the motors, batteries and cameras are of the same type as before

options.label: d
options.html: neither, because no new component has been invented

items.explanation_html: Slide 13: an architectural innovation changes the overall design of a system or the way its components interact with each other. The layout and the control of the drone change, even though the components are of the same type.

distractors.b: The definition is the right one for a component innovation, but the overall configuration of the drone does change, so it does not apply here.
distractors.c: Reusing the same type of components is compatible with an architectural innovation; what matters is the change in configuration and interaction.
distractors.d: An architectural innovation needs no new component: rearranging existing components into a new design is precisely what it covers.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B05 - Unit 7 Sources of Innovation and Design Dominance.md

items.title: Doubling effort on a mature technology
items.statement_html: The technology of a firm is already in the flat upper part of its S-curve of performance. If the firm doubles the effort it invests in that technology, what happens to performance:

options.label: a
options.html: It improves faster than ever, because the steepest part of the curve lies at the top

options.label: b
options.html: It doubles, because performance is proportional to effort

options.label: c
options.html: It falls, because the curve turns down after its maximum

options.label: d
options.html: It improves only a little, because the technology is approaching its limit

items.explanation_html: On the S-curve of technology performance (Slide 14), performance improves slowly, then quickly, and then flattens as it approaches the limit of the technology; near that limit additional effort brings small gains.

distractors.a: The steepest part of the S-curve is in the middle, not at the top, where the curve is flat.
distractors.b: Performance is not proportional to effort: the curve is S-shaped, not a straight line through the origin.
distractors.c: The S-curve does not turn down: it levels off at the limit of the technology drawn as a horizontal dotted line.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B05 - Unit 7 Sources of Innovation and Design Dominance.md

items.title: Arrival of a discontinuous technology
items.statement_html: Which one of the following statements about the introduction of a discontinuous technology is TRUE:

options.label: a
options.html: It always starts with a higher performance than the technology it replaces

options.label: b
options.html: It improves the components of the existing technology on the same knowledge base

options.label: c
options.html: It may start below the existing technology on its S-curve and later overtake it

options.label: d
options.html: It is the moment at which the diffusion of the existing technology reaches the laggards

items.explanation_html: A discontinuous technology fulfils a similar market need by building on an entirely new knowledge base; the technology S-curves of Slide 15 show that the second technology may start below the first one and later cross it.

distractors.a: Slide 15 (b) draws the second technology below the first at the beginning, so "always higher" contradicts the course figure.
distractors.b: Building on the same knowledge base describes an improvement of the existing technology, the opposite of an entirely new knowledge base.
distractors.d: The laggards are the last adopter category of the diffusion curve (Slide 16), a pattern of adoption over time, not the definition of a discontinuous technology.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B05 - Unit 7 Sources of Innovation and Design Dominance.md

items.title: Young, well educated and risk-oriented
items.statement_html: Which adopter category is described as a larger but still small group (13.5%) of risk-oriented individuals, highly adaptable to new technology, who follow the innovators and tend to be young and well educated:
items.explanation_html: Slide 16 describes the early adopters as a larger but still relatively small group, risk-oriented and highly adaptable to new technology, who follow the innovators and tend to be young and well educated; they are 13.5% of the population.

distractors.b: Innovators are the first 2.5%: leading-edge individuals extremely interested in technology, who come before the early adopters, not after them.
distractors.c: The early majority (34%) is much larger and more careful, waiting to see how new ideas are received before investing.
distractors.d: The late majority (34%) is slightly conservative and risk-averse and needs convincing, not risk-oriented.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B05 - Unit 7 Sources of Innovation and Design Dominance.md

items.title: Why a design wins
items.statement_html: Which pair of forces does the course give as the reasons why an industry selects a dominant design:

options.label: a
options.html: Official enforcement by a standards body and patent protection

items.explanation_html: Slides 18-19: learning effects (the more a technology is used, the more it is developed and the more efficient it becomes) and network externalities (the value to a user grows with the number of users, through the installed base and complementary goods) push the market towards a single design, which can produce winner-take-all markets.

distractors.a: A dominant design is a de facto standard: it need not be officially enforced (Slide 17), and patents are not among the reasons the course gives.
distractors.c: Spillovers and clusters describe how innovation arises in collaborative networks (Slide 9), not why one design comes to dominate a market.
distractors.d: Product and process are a pair of types of innovation (Slide 11); they classify innovations and do not explain the selection of a design.

items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Quiz - Bank B05 - Unit 7 Sources of Innovation and Design Dominance.md

items.title: Aldebaran Space Systems: IRR ranking against NPV at the cost of capital
items.source: Problem written for the bank in the style of Exercises 5 and 6 of BUSINESS_SECONDPARTIAL_2026_EXAMPLES_SOL.pdf; not an official exercise. Discount rate from the weighted cost of capital of Topic 3, Slide 37, as in 3_II_NPV IRR.pdf, Exercise 8; decision by Fisher's rate as in Exercise 9 of the same sheet.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Problem - Bank M01 - Aldebaran Space Systems IRR Ranking against NPV.md
items.statement_html:
Aldebaran Space Systems, a manufacturer of small satellites, is evaluating two investment projects:

  • Investment A: an automated integration line for satellite buses, requiring an initial outlay of 500,000 € and expected to generate net cash flows of 300,000 € in year 1 and 300,000 € in year 2.
  • Investment B: a test stand for reusable rocket engines with an unknown initial outlay, expected to generate net cash flows of 200,000 € in year 1 and 700,000 € in year 2.

The company is financed 40% with equity, whose cost is estimated at 9%, and 60% with liabilities, whose average cost is 4%. It uses the NPV criterion with its weighted average cost of capital as the yearly discount rate. The projects are mutually exclusive (only one can be accepted).

a) Determine the discount rate of the company and the maximum initial outlay of project B for it to be interesting (NPV ≥ 0). (0.5 points)

b) The initial outlay of project B is finally fixed at 750,000 €. Which investment is preferable under the IRR criterion? Does the NPV at the company's discount rate give the same ranking, and which project does the company undertake? (0.75 points)

c) A third project C is presented, a ground-station network for a satellite data-download service (a new line of business), requiring an initial investment of 200,000 € and generating 100,000 € in year 1 and 150,000 € in year 2. Draw a schematic graph of the NPV of the three projects as a function of the discount rate and compute Fisher's rates of the pairs A–B, A–C and B–C. (0.75 points)

d) Reason which project would be chosen depending on the discount rate, state from which discount rate no project should be selected, and say which project the company chooses at its own discount rate. (0.5 points)
items.setup_html:
Data

ProjectInitial outlay $A$ (€)$Q_1$ (€)$Q_2$ (€)
A500,000300,000300,000
Bunknown in (a); 750,000 from (b) on200,000700,000
C200,000100,000150,000
Financial structureShareCost
Equity $E$40%$K_{EQ}$ = 9%
Liabilities $L$60%$K_L$ = 4%

Model

  • Cost of capital (Topic 3, Slide 37): the capital cost is the weighted average of the costs of the financial resources, $K_{WACC} = K_{EQ}\,\frac{E}{E+L} + K_L\,\frac{L}{E+L}$. The key of 3_II_NPV IRR.pdf, Exercise 8 uses it as the cut-off rate of the IRR.
  • Net present value (Examples PDF, Exercise 5): with outlay $A$, flows $Q_t$ and discount rate $k$,
$$NPV = -A + \frac{Q_1}{1+k} + \frac{Q_2}{(1+k)^2}$$

A project is interesting when $NPV \geq 0$; of mutually exclusive projects, the one with the largest positive NPV is chosen.

  • Internal rate of return: the rate $r$ at which $NPV = 0$ (3_II_NPV_NPV IRR_solutions.pdf, Exercise 4). For a two-year project, with $x = 1 + r$ and multiplying by $x^2 > 0$, $NPV = 0$ becomes the quadratic $A\,x^2 - Q_1\,x - Q_2 = 0$, solved with $x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$. Only the root with $x > 0$ has economic meaning.
  • Fisher's rate of a pair: the rate at which both NPVs are equal (3_II_NPV_NPV IRR_solutions.pdf, Exercise 9). Multiplying $NPV_P = NPV_Q$ by $x^2$ gives $-A_P x^2 + Q_{1P} x + Q_{2P} = -A_Q x^2 + Q_{1Q} x + Q_{2Q}$, again a quadratic in $x$ (Examples PDF, Exercise 5 (c)).
  • Hypotheses: flows at the end of each year, a constant yearly discount rate, no taxes and no residual value.

subquestions.label: a
subquestions.prompt_html: Discount rate and maximum outlay of project B
subquestions.hint_html: First turn the financial structure into one rate with the weighted average of Slide 37. Then write the NPV of B with the outlay as the unknown $X$ and require $NPV_B \geq 0$.
subquestions.checkpoint_html:
• $K_{WACC}$ = 6.00%.
  • Present value of the flows of B at 6%: 811,676.75 €.
  • B is interesting for an outlay $X \leq$ 811,676.75 €.
subquestions.solution_html:
Discount rate from the financial structure

The weights are the shares of equity and liabilities in the financial structure, $E/(E+L) = 0.40$ and $L/(E+L) = 0.60$ (Topic 3, Slide 37):

$$K_{WACC} = 0.40 \times 9\% + 0.60 \times 4\% = 3.60\% + 2.40\% = 6.00\%$$

So $k = 0.06$ and the discount factors are $1 + k = 1.06$ and $(1 + k)^2 = 1.06 \times 1.06 = 1.1236$.

NPV of B with an unknown outlay

Writing every term of the NPV of B with outlay $X$:

$$NPV_B = -X + \frac{200{,}000}{1.06} + \frac{700{,}000}{1.1236} = -X + 188{,}679.245 + 622{,}997.508 = -X + 811{,}676.75$$

Condition NPV ≥ 0

$$-X + 811{,}676.75 \geq 0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad X \leq 811{,}676.75\ \text{€}$$

Project B is interesting as long as its initial outlay does not exceed 811,676.75 €, the present value of its flows at 6%. Units: each term is a sum of money in € divided by a dimensionless factor $(1.06)^t$, so the NPV is in €.

subquestions.label: b
subquestions.prompt_html: IRR ranking of A and B, and the NPV at the cost of capital
subquestions.hint_html: Set each NPV equal to zero, put $x = 1 + r$, multiply by $x^2$ and solve the quadratic; keep the positive root. Then compute both NPVs at 6% and compare the two rankings.
subquestions.checkpoint_html:
• IRR(A) = 13.07%; IRR(B) = 10.86%; both above 6%, and A ranks first by IRR.
  • $NPV_A(6\%)$ = 50,017.80 €; $NPV_B(6\%)$ = 61,676.75 €; B ranks first by NPV.
  • The company uses NPV, so it undertakes B (the conflict is explained by Fisher's rate A–B in (c)).
subquestions.solution_html:
IRR of A

$$-500{,}000 + \frac{300{,}000}{x} + \frac{300{,}000}{x^2} = 0 \quad\xrightarrow{\ \times x^2\ }\quad 500{,}000\,x^2 - 300{,}000\,x - 300{,}000 = 0$$

Dividing by 100,000: $5x^2 - 3x - 3 = 0$, with $a = 5$, $b = -3$, $c = -3$:

$$x = \frac{3 \pm \sqrt{(-3)^2 - 4 \cdot 5 \cdot (-3)}}{2 \cdot 5} = \frac{3 \pm \sqrt{9 + 60}}{10} = \frac{3 \pm \sqrt{69}}{10} = \frac{3 \pm 8.30662}{10}$$

The roots are $x = 1.130662$ and $x = -0.530662$; the negative one has no economic meaning. Hence $r_A = 1.130662 - 1 = 0.1307$, IRR(A) = 13.07%.

IRR of B

$$-750{,}000 + \frac{200{,}000}{x} + \frac{700{,}000}{x^2} = 0 \quad\xrightarrow{\ \times x^2\ }\quad 750{,}000\,x^2 - 200{,}000\,x - 700{,}000 = 0$$

Dividing by 50,000: $15x^2 - 4x - 14 = 0$, with $a = 15$, $b = -4$, $c = -14$:

$$x = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{(-4)^2 - 4 \cdot 15 \cdot (-14)}}{2 \cdot 15} = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{16 + 840}}{30} = \frac{4 \pm \sqrt{856}}{30} = \frac{4 \pm 29.25748}{30}$$

The positive root is $x = 1.108583$ (the other, $-0.841916$, is rejected), so IRR(B) = 10.86%.

Ranking by IRR

Both IRRs exceed the 6% cost of capital, so each project is acceptable on its own (IRR > k, 3_II_NPV IRR.pdf, Exercise 8). Under the IRR criterion A is preferable, because $13.07\% > 10.86\%$.

NPVs at the company's discount rate

$$NPV_A(6\%) = -500{,}000 + \frac{300{,}000}{1.06} + \frac{300{,}000}{1.1236} = -500{,}000 + 283{,}018.868 + 266{,}998.932 = 50{,}017.80\ \text{€}$$
$$NPV_B(6\%) = -750{,}000 + 188{,}679.245 + 622{,}997.508 = 61{,}676.75\ \text{€}$$

(the two discounted terms of B are those of part (a); equivalently $811{,}676.75 - 750{,}000$).

The two rankings disagree

At 6% the NPV ranks B first ($61{,}676.75 > 50{,}017.80$), the opposite of the IRR ranking. The company has adopted the NPV criterion and the projects are mutually exclusive, so it undertakes B. The IRR compares the projects at their own break-even rates, not at the company's 6%; B receives most of its money in year 2, so its NPV is high when the rate is low and falls fast when the rate rises. Part (c) shows that the two NPV profiles cross at Fisher's rate A–B of 8.06%, above the 6% of the company.

subquestions.label: c
subquestions.prompt_html: NPV profiles and Fisher's rates of the three pairs
subquestions.hint_html: For each project, mark the NPV at 0% (the plain sum of flows minus the outlay) on the vertical axis and the IRR on the horizontal axis. For each pair, equate the two NPVs, multiply by $x^2$ and solve the quadratic in $x = 1 + r$.

subquestions.label: d
subquestions.prompt_html: Decision intervals and the rate above which no project is chosen
subquestions.hint_html: Follow the highest of the three profiles from left to right: it changes only at a Fisher's rate where the two leading profiles cross, and the choice ends at the largest IRR.
subquestions.checkpoint_html:
• $0 \leq r < 8.06\%$: B; $8.06\% < r < 11.51\%$: A; $11.51\% < r < 15.14\%$: C; $r > 15.14\%$: no project.
  • At the company's 6%: project B.
  • The B–C crossing at 9.50% happens while A is ahead of both, so it changes nothing.
subquestions.solution_html:
The upper envelope of the three profiles

  • From 0% to 8.06%, B is above A (A–B) and above C (B–C holds up to 9.50%): B.
  • At 8.06% A overtakes B. Between 8.06% and 11.51%, A is above B (A–B) and above C (A–C): A. The B–C crossing at 9.50% lies inside this interval, below A, so it does not change the decision.
  • At 11.51% C overtakes A, and C is already above B (since 9.50%). Between 11.51% and 15.14%, C has the largest NPV and it is positive: C.
  • Above 15.14%, the largest IRR, every NPV is negative: no project should be selected.

Check at one rate inside each interval: at 4%, $NPV_A$ = 65,828.40 €, $NPV_B$ = 89,497.04 €, $NPV_C$ = 34,837.28 € (B); at 10%, 20,661.16 €, 10,330.58 € and 14,876.03 € (A); at 14%, −6,001.85 €, −35,934.13 € and 3,139.43 € (C); at 16%, −18,430.44 €, −57,372.18 € and −2,318.67 € (none).

Decision of the company

$$0\% \leq r < 8.06\% \Rightarrow B, \qquad 8.06\% < r < 11.51\% \Rightarrow A, \qquad 11.51\% < r < 15.14\% \Rightarrow C, \qquad r > 15.14\% \Rightarrow \text{no project}$$

At exactly a Fisher's rate the two leading projects are indifferent. At its own discount rate of 6%, Aldebaran chooses project B. The trap is twofold: A beats B by IRR, and C has the highest IRR of the three, yet at 6% C has the lowest NPV (27,839.09 €). The IRR ranking only tells which project survives longest as the rate rises; at a given cost of capital the decision follows the NPV.

items.interpretation_html: The three profiles differ in how their money is spread over time. B concentrates 700,000 € in year 2, so a rising rate hits it hardest: it leads at low rates and is the first to drop out. C is small and returns most of its outlay in year 1, so its profile is flat and it is the last to become negative. Limiting cases: at $r = 0$ the NPV is the plain sum of flows minus the outlay, and as $r \to \infty$ every discounted flow tends to 0, so the NPV tends to minus the outlay. Dimensions: every NPV is a sum of amounts in € divided by dimensionless factors, so it is in €; the IRR and Fisher's rates are dimensionless rates per year. A common exam mistake is to stop at "A has the higher IRR, so A is chosen" without comparing the NPVs at the company's own rate, which here lies below Fisher's rate A–B.

items.title: Helix Composites: break-even list price with a discount for one customer, profit margin target, leverage and a price cut
items.source: Problem written for the bank in the style of Exercise 1 of BUSINESS_SECONDPARTIAL_2026_EXAMPLES_SOL.pdf; not an official exercise. Method: Topic 4, Slides 37-42; Topic 5, Slide 17 and topic 5.2.2.pdf, pp. 2-3.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Problem - Bank M02 - Helix Composites Break-Even with an OEM Discount.md
items.statement_html:
Helix Composites S.L. manufactures carbon-fibre rotor blades for cargo drones. Its expected annual costs are:

  • Lease of the autoclave hall: 380,000 €
  • Salaries of the lay-up operators, hired on fixed annual contracts: 460,000 €
  • Salaries of the engineering and quality staff: 200,000 €
  • Depreciation of the moulds and the autoclave: 100,000 €
  • Insurance and administration: 60,000 €
  • Interest on the bank loan that financed the autoclave: 60,000 €
  • Carbon prepreg and resin: 36 € per blade
  • Autoclave energy: 7 € per blade
  • Packaging and transport to the customer: 5 € per blade

The sales forecast is 25,000 blades a year. 40% of the blades are sold to one drone manufacturer (OEM) under a framework contract that gives it a 10% discount on the list price; the other customers buy the remaining 60% at the list price.

a) Classify the costs and calculate the list price per blade that makes the firm break even (zero operating profit) at the forecast volume of 25,000 blades. (0.5 points)

b) Using the list price found in (a), calculate the volume of blades the firm must sell to earn an operating profit equal to 10% of its net sales revenue. (0.5 points)

c) Calculate the operating leverage (OL) at the volume found in (b) and at a volume of 40,000 blades. What do these values mean? (0.75 points)

d) At 40,000 blades the price elasticity of demand is 1.5. The firm cuts its list price by 4%, keeping the OEM discount and the share of each group of customers. Calculate the new expected volume, the new operating profit and the change in sales revenue, and explain the result. (0.75 points)
items.setup_html:
ItemValue
Forecast volume$Q = 25{,}000$ blades
Share of the OEM (10% discount)40% of the units
Share of the other customers (list price)60% of the units
Target of part (b)operating profit = 10% of net sales revenue
Second volume of part (c)40,000 blades
Price elasticity at 40,000 blades$E_d = 1.5$ (absolute value)
Change of the list price in part (d)−4%

Model of the course:

  • Profit $= P\,Q - (VC\,Q + FC) = Q\,(P - VC) - FC$, unit margin $m = P - VC$, break-even point $Q_0 = FC/m$ (Topic 4, Slide 37).
  • Operating leverage $OL = Q\,m/(Q\,m - FC) = Q/(Q - Q^*)$ (Topic 4, Slides 39, 40 and 42).
  • Price elasticity $E_d = (\Delta Q/Q)/(\Delta P/P)$, used in absolute value, so $\Delta Q/Q = -E_d\,\Delta P/P$ (Topic 5, Slide 17; topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 2), as in Examples PDF, Exercise 1 (d).

subquestions.label: a
subquestions.prompt_html: Classify the costs and find the break-even list price
subquestions.hint_html: A cost is fixed when its yearly amount does not depend on the number of blades. Revenue is earned at the average net price that the two groups of customers pay, not at the list price. Ask whether the interest on the loan is an operating cost.
subquestions.checkpoint_html:
• $FC$ = 1,200,000 €; $VC$ = 48 € per blade; the interest (60,000 €) is not an operating cost
  • Average net price = 0.96 × list price
  • Net price = 96 € per blade; list price = 100 € per blade
subquestions.solution_html:
Classify the costs

The lease, the salaries of the operators (fixed annual contracts, as the direct labour of Examples PDF, Exercise 1), the salaries of the engineering and quality staff, the depreciation and the insurance and administration are the same whatever the number of blades: they are fixed costs.

$$FC = 380{,}000 + 460{,}000 + 200{,}000 + 100{,}000 + 60{,}000 = 1{,}200{,}000\ \text{€}$$

The prepreg and resin, the energy of the autoclave and the packaging and transport are spent once per blade: they are variable costs per unit.

$$VC = 36 + 7 + 5 = 48\ \text{€/blade}$$

The interest on the bank loan is a financial expense, a non-operating item of the income statement (Topic 3, Slide 11): it lies below the operating profit (EBIT) and does not enter a break-even point defined on the operating profit. It is left out of $FC$.

Average net price

Of every 100 blades, 40 are sold at $0.90\,P_L$ (list price minus the 10% discount) and 60 at $P_L$. The average net price per blade is the weighted mean:

$$P = 0.40 \times 0.90\,P_L + 0.60 \times P_L = (0.36 + 0.60)\,P_L = 0.96\,P_L$$

Break-even condition at 25,000 blades

At the break-even point revenue equals total cost, $P\,Q_0 = FC + VC\,Q_0$ (Topic 4, Slide 37). Solving for the net price:

$$P = \frac{FC + VC\,Q_0}{Q_0} = \frac{1{,}200{,}000 + 48 \times 25{,}000}{25{,}000} = \frac{2{,}400{,}000}{25{,}000} = 96\ \text{€/blade}$$

From the net price to the list price

$$P_L = \frac{P}{0.96} = \frac{96}{0.96} = 100\ \text{€/blade}$$

Check: $m = 96 - 48 = 48$ € and $Q_0 = FC/m = 1{,}200{,}000/48 = 25{,}000$ blades, the forecast volume. Units: € divided by € per blade gives blades. Had the interest been counted as a fixed cost, the net price would be $(1{,}260{,}000 + 1{,}200{,}000)/25{,}000 = 98.4$ € and the list price 102.5 €; had the discount been applied to all customers, as in Pegasus, the list price would be $96/0.90 = 106.67$ €.

subquestions.label: b
subquestions.prompt_html: Volume for an operating profit of 10% of net sales
subquestions.hint_html: Write the target as an equation in $Q$: the profit $Q\,m - FC$ must equal 10% of the revenue $P\,Q$. The target profit is not a fixed number, so $Q = (\text{Profit} + FC)/m$ cannot be used directly.
subquestions.checkpoint_html:
• Unit margin $m$ = 48 € per blade, 10% of the net price = 9.60 € per blade
  • $Q$ = 31,250 blades
  • Revenue 3,000,000 €, operating profit 300,000 €
subquestions.solution_html:
Set the target as an equation

With the list price of 100 €, the net price is $P = 96$ € and $m = P - VC = 96 - 48 = 48$ € per blade. The target is

$$Q\,m - FC = 0.10 \times P\,Q$$

Solve for the volume

Move the terms in $Q$ to the left and factor $Q$:

$$Q\,(m - 0.10\,P) = FC \quad\Longrightarrow\quad Q = \frac{FC}{m - 0.10\,P} = \frac{1{,}200{,}000}{48 - 0.10 \times 96} = \frac{1{,}200{,}000}{38.40} = 31{,}250\ \text{blades}$$

Each blade leaves 48 € of margin, of which 9.60 € must be kept as profit, so only 38.40 € per blade is left to cover the fixed costs.

Check

Revenue $= 96 \times 31{,}250 = 3{,}000{,}000$ €. Operating profit $= 31{,}250 \times 48 - 1{,}200{,}000 = 1{,}500{,}000 - 1{,}200{,}000 = 300{,}000$ €, which is $300{,}000/3{,}000{,}000 = 10\%$ of the revenue. The volume is above the break-even point (25,000 blades), as a positive profit requires.

subquestions.label: c
subquestions.prompt_html: Operating leverage at 31,250 and at 40,000 blades
subquestions.hint_html: Use $OL = Q\,m/(Q\,m - FC)$ and check it with $OL = Q/(Q - Q^*)$, where $Q^*$ is the break-even point of part (a).
subquestions.checkpoint_html:
• At 31,250 blades: $Q\,m$ = 1,500,000 €, profit 300,000 €, OL = 5.00
  • At 40,000 blades: $Q\,m$ = 1,920,000 €, profit 720,000 €, OL = 2.67
  • Meaning: a 1% change in sales changes the operating profit by 5% and by 2.67%
subquestions.solution_html:
Leverage at 31,250 blades

$$OL = \frac{Q\,m}{Q\,m - FC} = \frac{31{,}250 \times 48}{31{,}250 \times 48 - 1{,}200{,}000} = \frac{1{,}500{,}000}{300{,}000} = 5.00$$

Check with the break-even point, $Q^* = 25{,}000$ (Topic 4, Slide 42): $OL = 31{,}250/(31{,}250 - 25{,}000) = 31{,}250/6{,}250 = 5.00$.

Leverage at 40,000 blades

$$OL = \frac{40{,}000 \times 48}{40{,}000 \times 48 - 1{,}200{,}000} = \frac{1{,}920{,}000}{720{,}000} = 2.67$$

Check: $OL = 40{,}000/(40{,}000 - 25{,}000) = 40{,}000/15{,}000 = 2.67$.

Meaning

The OL measures how a change in sales translates into a change in operating profit (Topic 4, Slide 40). At 31,250 blades a 1% change in sales changes the operating profit by 5% in the same direction (a 10% fall in sales would cut profit by 50%); at 40,000 blades the same 1% changes the profit by only 2.67%. Both values are greater than 1 because the firm has profits ($Q > Q^*$), and the leverage falls as the volume moves away from the break-even point (Topic 4, Slide 42). The OL is an index of economic risk (Topic 4, Slide 41): Helix is riskier at 31,250 blades, close to its break-even point, than at 40,000. The leverage is a pure number: € over €, or blades over blades.

subquestions.label: d
subquestions.prompt_html: A 4% cut in the list price with an elasticity of 1.5
subquestions.hint_html: Because the discount is a percentage and the customer mix does not change, the average net price falls by the same 4% as the list price. Apply $\Delta Q/Q = -E_d\,\Delta P/P$ at the starting point of 40,000 blades, then recompute margin and profit.
subquestions.checkpoint_html:
• $\Delta Q/Q$ = +6%, new volume 42,400 blades
  • New net price 92.16 €, new margin 44.16 €
  • New operating profit 672,384 € (was 720,000 €: −47,616 €)
  • Revenue rises from 3,840,000 € to 3,907,584 € (+67,584 €)
subquestions.solution_html:
New volume

The relative change of the list price is $\Delta P/P = -4\% = -0.04$. With $E_d = 1.5$ in absolute value (Topic 5, Slide 17; topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 2):

$$\frac{\Delta Q}{Q} = -E_d\,\frac{\Delta P}{P} = -1.5 \times (-0.04) = +0.06$$
$$Q_{new} = 40{,}000 \times (1 + 0.06) = 42{,}400\ \text{blades}$$

New net price and margin

The average net price is $0.96\,P_L$, so it changes in the same proportion as the list price:

$$P_{new} = 96 \times (1 - 0.04) = 92.16\ \text{€/blade} \qquad m_{new} = 92.16 - 48 = 44.16\ \text{€/blade}$$

(New list price $100 \times 0.96 = 96$ €; $0.96 \times 96 = 92.16$ €, the same result.)

New operating profit

$$\text{Profit}_{new} = Q_{new}\,m_{new} - FC = 42{,}400 \times 44.16 - 1{,}200{,}000 = 1{,}872{,}384 - 1{,}200{,}000 = 672{,}384\ \text{€}$$

Before the price cut: $\text{Profit} = 40{,}000 \times 48 - 1{,}200{,}000 = 720{,}000$ €. The profit falls by $720{,}000 - 672{,}384 = 47{,}616$ €.

Revenue and explanation

Revenue before: $40{,}000 \times 96 = 3{,}840{,}000$ €. Revenue after: $42{,}400 \times 92.16 = 3{,}907{,}584$ €, a rise of 67,584 €. The demand is elastic ($E_d > 1$), so a price cut raises the volume more than proportionally and the revenue rises (topic 5.2.2.pdf, p. 3). The operating profit, however, falls: the unit margin drops from 48 € to 44.16 €, a fall of $3.84/48 = 8\%$, twice the 4% price cut because the variable cost does not fall, and the 6% gain in volume does not make up for it. Higher revenue does not mean higher profit; the decision must be judged on the margin.

items.interpretation_html: Helix's break-even list price (100 €) already includes the fact that only 40% of the blades carry the discount, which lowers the average price by 4% instead of 10%. The leverage falls from 5.00 to 2.67 as the firm moves from 31,250 to 40,000 blades, so further away from its break-even point its profit is less sensitive to sales. The price cut of part (d) is the opposite of the price rise of Pegasus: with elastic demand it gains revenue but loses operating profit, because each blade sold earns 3.84 € less while the fixed costs stay at 1,200,000 €. Limiting cases: with no OEM customers the factor 0.96 becomes 1 and the list price would be 96 €; at $Q = Q^* = 25{,}000$ the OL is not defined (the profit is zero). Dimensions: prices and margins in € per blade, volumes in blades, profits and revenues in €, OL and elasticity dimensionless.

verify.label: (b) volume for a 10% margin on sales

items.title: VectraSky survey drones: strategic marketing, product, range and distribution
items.source: Problem written for the bank in the style of Exercise 2 of BUSINESS_SECONDPARTIAL_2026_EXAMPLES_SOL.pdf; the company and its facts are invented; not an official exercise.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Problem - Bank M03 - VectraSky Survey Drones Marketing Strategy.md
items.statement_html:
VectraSky is a Portuguese company founded in 2016 in Porto that designs and builds small fixed-wing drones for surveying crops and forests. Before launching its first model, the founders studied the drone market and its competitors: the large manufacturers were focused on hobby users and film-makers, while medium-sized farms and forestry cooperatives in southern Europe had no affordable aircraft able to survey a whole estate in one flight. VectraSky decided to serve only these farms and cooperatives, and its slogan, "The whole farm on one charge", presents its drones as the long-endurance option at a moderate price.

The drones carry the VectraSky name and a green swallow as logo. The wings fold so that the aircraft fits in the boot of a car, it is ready to fly in under five minutes, and it is flown from a tablet application with large buttons that can be used with work gloves. Every airframe is sealed against dust and rain and is flown for 20 hours in the factory before delivery, and the drone comes with a three-year warranty. It is delivered in a rugged, reusable transport case whose label gives the operating instructions in four languages. After the sale, VectraSky ships any spare part within 48 hours and trains the customer's pilots on site. To make itself known, the firm runs flight demonstrations at agricultural fairs and places advertisements in farming magazines.

The current range has two product lines: survey drones (Field 60, Field 90 and Forest 120) and sensor payloads (a multispectral camera and a thermal camera); every product is used for the aerial survey of crops and forests. VectraSky does not sell to its customers directly: its drones are sold by agricultural-machinery dealers, who resell them to the farms and cooperatives. The firm chooses at most two dealers in each region, and only dealers that have a workshop able to repair the drones.

a) Which elements of the strategic marketing approach appear in the text? Identify at least three and justify each with a fact of the text. (0.75 points)

b) Which product attribute strategy does VectraSky follow? Identify at least four attributes, and say which facts of the text are not product attributes. (0.75 points)

c) Describe the range of products of VectraSky (extension or width, depth, length and consistency), and say which characteristics change if the firm adds a Field 75 model to its drone line. (0.5 points)

d) Which distribution strategy does VectraSky follow? Describe the type and length of the channel, whether it is B2B or B2C, and the distribution intensity. (0.5 points)

subquestions.label: a
subquestions.prompt_html: Elements of the strategic marketing approach in the text
subquestions.hint_html: Strategic marketing is the analysis system: analysis of the situation, diagnosis, objective, and the strategies of segmentation and positioning. Look in the first paragraph for each of them.
subquestions.checkpoint_html:
• Analysis of the situation: market and competitors' analysis (the founders "studied the drone market and its competitors").
  • Market segmentation and targeting: medium-sized farms and forestry cooperatives in southern Europe, a single segment (differentiated concentrated, niche strategy), identified as an unmet need.
  • Positioning: "The whole farm on one charge", long endurance at a moderate price (benefits of the product, price-quality relationship).
  • Customer orientation (market orientation): the product is designed for the needs of the chosen customers.
subquestions.solution_html:
Analysis of the situation

"The founders studied the drone market and its competitors": this is the first stage of strategic marketing, the analysis of the situation (market analysis and competitors' analysis) [Topic 5, Slide 7]. The finding that the large manufacturers left farms and cooperatives without an affordable long-endurance aircraft is an opportunity in the sense of the slide: segmentation identifies the market needs that are not being satisfied [Topic 5, Slide 11].

Market segmentation and targeting

"Medium-sized farms and forestry cooperatives in southern Europe" defines a segment with a geographical criterion (southern Europe) and a criterion of type of use of the product (surveying crops and forests) [Topic 5, Slide 10]. "VectraSky decided to serve only these farms and cooperatives": the firm aims its product and its message at a single, well-defined segment, the differentiated concentrated (niche) strategy [Topic 5, Slide 12].

Positioning

"The whole farm on one charge ... the long-endurance option at a moderate price" is the image the firm wants to create in the mind of the target customer: positioning [Topic 5, Slide 13]. It is based on a benefit of the product (surveying a whole estate in one flight) and on the price-quality relationship [Topic 5, Slide 14]. Positioning is a strategic decision, not an operative one [Examples PDF, Exercise 4, statement 1].

Customer orientation

The whole offer starts from what the chosen customers need, which is the market (customer) orientation of the active marketing stage: producing what potential customers want [Topic 5, Slide 4]. Three of these four elements, each with its fact of the text, earn the full marks.

subquestions.label: b
subquestions.prompt_html: Product attribute strategy
subquestions.hint_html: The psychosocial attributes of the product are brand, design, packaging and quality; warranty and post-sale service are further attributes. Promotion is a different element of the marketing mix.
subquestions.checkpoint_html:
• Brand: name VectraSky and a green swallow as logo.
  • Design: folding wings, fits in a car boot, ready in under five minutes, tablet application usable with gloves (aesthetic and functional).
  • Quality: sealed against dust and rain, 20 hours of factory flight before delivery.
  • Packaging: rugged reusable transport case with the instructions in four languages on its label.
  • Warranty and post-sale service: three-year warranty, spare parts in 48 hours, on-site pilot training.
  • Not product attributes: flight demonstrations at fairs and advertisements in farming magazines belong to the promotion (communication) policy.
subquestions.solution_html:
The attributes found in the text

The product is a bundle of tangible and intangible attributes; besides the basic product the customer buys quality, design, packaging, post-sale services and image, and the psychosocial attributes are brand, design, packaging and quality [Topic 5, Slide 19].

Fact of the textAttribute of the course
"The VectraSky name and a green swallow as logo"Brand: a name (the part that can be said) and a logo (design, symbol, colours) [Topic 5, Slide 20]
"The wings fold ... fits in the boot of a car ... ready to fly in under five minutes ... large buttons that can be used with work gloves"Design, from the functional perspective of ease of use [Topic 5, Slide 22]
"Sealed against dust and rain ... flown for 20 hours in the factory before delivery"Quality: the product satisfies the needs of customers who fly in the field [Topic 5, Slide 23]
"Rugged, reusable transport case whose label gives the operating instructions in four languages"Packaging: it protects the content, eases transport and carries the label with information [Topic 5, Slide 22]
"Three-year warranty ... spare part within 48 hours ... trains the customer's pilots on site"Warranty and post-sale services [Topic 5, Slide 23]

Four of these attributes, each with its fact, earn the full marks.

What is not a product attribute

"Flight demonstrations at agricultural fairs" and "advertisements in farming magazines" are not attributes of the product: they belong to the promotion (communication) policy of the marketing mix, the first as an activity close to personal selling and public relations at the fairs, the second as advertising, a paid, non-personal communication through the mass media [Topic 5, Slides 29-30]. The examples PDF draws the same line: communication is not a product attribute [Examples PDF, Exercise 2 (b)].

subquestions.label: c
subquestions.prompt_html: The range of products and the effect of a new model
subquestions.hint_html: Count the lines, the products in each line and the products in total. Then ask which of the counts a new model inside an existing line changes.
subquestions.checkpoint_html:
• Extension (width): 2 lines.
  • Depth: 3 drones and 2 payloads.
  • Length: 5 products.
  • Consistency: high, every product serves the aerial survey of crops and forests.
  • Field 75: depth of the drone line 3 to 4, length 5 to 6; extension (width) and consistency unchanged.
subquestions.solution_html:
Characteristics of the current range

A range of products is an offer of product lines and individual products, described by its extension, depth, length and consistency [Topic 5, Slide 24]. The examples PDF calls the extension the width (breadth) of the range [Examples PDF, Exercise 4, statement 3].

CharacteristicDefinitionVectraSky
Extension (width)number of product lines2 (survey drones, sensor payloads)
Depthnumber of products per line3 drones; 2 payloads
Lengthtotal number of individual products$3 + 2 = 5$
Consistencyrelation of the products with their final usehigh: every product is used "for the aerial survey of crops and forests"

A Field 75 model

The Field 75 enters the existing drone line, which is the strategy "extend the product lines" [Topic 5, Slide 24]: the depth of the drone line rises from 3 to 4 and the length of the range from 5 to 6. The extension (width) stays at 2, because no new line is created, and the consistency stays high, because the new drone has the same final use.

subquestions.label: d
subquestions.prompt_html: Distribution strategy
subquestions.hint_html: Ask who sells to the final buyer, how many intermediaries stand between the producer and that buyer, whether the buyer is a firm or a consumer, and how many outlets there are in each region.
subquestions.checkpoint_html:
• Indirect channel: independent agricultural-machinery dealers.
  • Short channel with one level of intermediaries: producer, dealer, farm.
  • B2B: the final buyers are farms and cooperatives, which are firms.
  • Selective intensity: at most two chosen dealers per region, with a repair workshop.
subquestions.solution_html:
Type and length of the channel

"VectraSky does not sell to its customers directly: its drones are sold by agricultural-machinery dealers": the producer entrusts the sale to independent intermediaries, so the channel is indirect [Topic 5, Slide 35]. One intermediary stands between the producer and the final buyer (producer, dealer, farm), a short channel of one level. Extension: the level of a channel is the number of intermediaries between the producer and the final buyer; the examples PDF calls a channel with none a zero-level channel [Examples PDF, Exercise 2 (c)].

B2B and intensity

The final buyers, farms and forestry cooperatives, are firms, so the market is business-to-business (B2B), as in the TechNova case [Examples PDF, Exercise 2 (c)]. "At most two dealers in each region, and only dealers that have a workshop able to repair the drones" is selective distribution, one of the three strategies of Slide 37 [Topic 5, Slide 37]. Extension (definitions not given on the slide): intensive distribution uses as many outlets as possible, selective distribution a limited number of chosen outlets per area, and exclusive distribution a single outlet per area. The workshop requirement shows the criteria of the choice: the characteristics of the product (it needs repairs) and of each intermediary [Topic 5, Slide 37].

items.interpretation_html: Every decision of VectraSky follows from its strategic choice. A single segment (farms and cooperatives that survey large areas) explains the long-endurance design, the rugged case and the field service; a short, selective channel of dealers with workshops keeps that service close to the customer without the cost of an own sales network.

items.title: Altair MRO introduces a digital maintenance platform
items.source: Case written for the bank in the style of Exercise 3 of BUSINESS_SECONDPARTIAL_2026_EXAMPLES_SOL.pdf; not an official exercise. Content from Topic 6, Slides 3-8, 13-16, 18, 20, 22-25.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Problem - Bank M04 - Altair MRO Digital Maintenance Platform.md
items.statement_html:
Altair MRO is a maintenance, repair and overhaul company with 600 employees and three hangars that service regional aircraft. Today every inspection and repair is recorded on paper task cards; the cards travel by hand to the planning office, aircraft often leave the hangar late because a card or a spare part is missing, and the airlines that are its customers complain that they only learn about delays at the last minute.

The Chief Executive Officer wants to replace the paper cards with a digital maintenance platform: technicians would record each task on a tablet at the aircraft, the stock of spare parts would update automatically, and the airline would follow the progress of its aircraft online. The firm has never used such a system and no competitor of its size has one. The firm is organized by functions (inspection, repair, planning, stores), each with its own head; every procedure is written in detailed manuals, there are six hierarchical levels between the technician and the CEO, and any change to a procedure must be approved by the technical director.

Tasks:

a) Describe at least one task that should be performed in each of the four managerial functions to introduce the platform. (0.5 points)

b) List the steps of the decision-making process the CEO should follow, applying each one to the case. (0.5 points)

c) Classify the decision to adopt the platform by type of decision and by management level, and say which basic managerial skill weighs most for the manager who takes it. (0.5 points)

d) Define four KPIs (Key Performance Indicators) to control the introduction of the platform. (0.5 points)

e) Using the basic organizational configurations of Mintzberg, state in which one the platform would be hardest to introduce and in which one easiest, justifying each answer with the features of the configuration. (0.5 points)

subquestions.label: a
subquestions.prompt_html: One task per managerial function
subquestions.hint_html: The four functions of the course are planning, organizing, leading and controlling. In the course, leading is human resources management (directing and staffing), and controlling measures results against the standards set when planning.
subquestions.checkpoint_html:
• Planning: objectives and calendar of the roll-out (goal with a date, forecasts, alternatives, chosen course of action).
  • Organizing: who does what, a project team, new tasks and their coordination, the organization chart updated.
  • Leading: motivation, communication and training of technicians; recruiting and selecting new profiles if needed.
  • Controlling: standards, measurement, deviations, corrective action.
subquestions.solution_html:
Planning

Planning is setting goals and deciding on the strategy to achieve them, and a goal is a specific achievement to be attained at a future date (Topic 6, Slide 10). Task: set the objective "all three hangars working without paper task cards within twelve months", forecast the cost and the training time, compare a gradual roll-out (one hangar first) with a simultaneous one, and fix the calendar of the chosen option.

Organizing

Organizing arranges the human resources so that their activities contribute to the firm's goals, through differentiation (dividing the work) and integration (coordinating it) (Topic 6, Slide 11). Task: create a project team with members of inspection, repair, planning and stores, give each member a distinct task (data migration, tablet set-up, rewriting the procedures), name one person per hangar to coordinate, and update the organization chart with the new roles.

Leading

Leading is human resources management (Topic 6, Slides 2 and 23): directing (motivation, leadership, communication) and staffing (recruiting, selecting, training, appraisal and compensation). Task: explain to the technicians why the paper cards are being replaced, train every technician on the tablets, and recruit and then select a data specialist if nobody in the firm can run the platform. Recruitment (attracting candidates) comes before selection (choosing among them).

Controlling

Controlling ensures that activities provide the planned results: establishing standards, measuring actual performance, identifying deviations and taking corrective action (Topic 6, Slide 24). Task: compare every month the progress of the roll-out with the calendar set when planning, measure the KPIs of part (d), and correct the deviations (more training in a hangar that lags behind, for example). Buying the tablets is an operation of the project, not a managerial function in itself.

subquestions.label: b
subquestions.prompt_html: The decision-making process applied to the case
subquestions.hint_html: The course gives eight steps, in a fixed order, from recognizing the problem to implementing changes.
subquestions.checkpoint_html:
• The eight steps in the order of the course, each applied to Altair MRO.
  • Analysis (step 4) before choice (step 5); evaluation (step 7) before changes (step 8).
subquestions.solution_html:
The eight steps in the case

The decision-making process has eight steps (Topic 6, Slide 6):

  1. Recognizing the problem or opportunity: aircraft leave late because paper cards and spare parts go missing, and customers learn about delays at the last minute.
  2. Gathering information, identifying the critical factors: how many delays come from lost cards or missing parts, how many technicians and aircraft are involved, the budget, and what the airlines expect.
  3. Considering alternative courses of action: keep paper but add a courier between hangar and office; scan the cards at the end of each shift; adopt the full digital platform.
  4. Analysing the alternatives: cost, time to introduce, training needed and expected reduction of delays of each one.
  5. Choosing an alternative: the digital platform, the only one that updates stock and informs the customer in real time.
  6. Implementing the decision: the roll-out planned and organized in part (a).
  7. Evaluating the results: compare delays and customer complaints before and after, with the KPIs of part (d).
  8. Implementing changes: adjust the platform, the procedures or the training where the evaluation shows deviations.

subquestions.label: c
subquestions.prompt_html: Type of decision, management level and skill
subquestions.hint_html: Slide 5 classifies decisions by the type of problem and of alternatives; Slide 7 places the decisions on the management pyramid; Slide 8 shows which skill weighs most at each level.
subquestions.checkpoint_html:
• Innovative (not planned) decision: new and ambiguous problem, unplanned alternatives; quote "never used such a system", "no competitor of its size".
  • Top management, strategic and general decision.
  • Conceptual skill, the ability to see the firm as a whole.
subquestions.solution_html:
Type of decision

The firm "has never used such a system and no competitor of its size has one": the problem is unusual and the alternatives are ambiguous and not planned, so this is an innovative (not planned) decision, not a routine one, which would face a known, well-defined problem with known alternatives (Topic 6, Slide 5).

Management level

The platform changes the way the three hangars, the stores and the relation with the customers work: it affects the firm as a whole, so it is a strategic, general decision of top management (the CEO), not a tactical decision of middle management or an operational one of first-line supervisors (Topic 6, Slide 7; Examples PDF, Exercise 4, statement 5). Choosing which hangar team is trained first on Monday would, by contrast, be an operational decision.

Skill

The skill that weighs most in top management is the conceptual skill, the ability to see the firm as a whole: the CEO must see how the platform links maintenance, stores, planning and customers. Technical skill weighs most in low management (Topic 6, Slide 8).

subquestions.label: d
subquestions.prompt_html: Four KPIs to control the introduction
subquestions.hint_html: A KPI (Key Performance Indicator) is a measurable indicator of whether an objective is being achieved; it is the measure of actual performance that controlling compares with a standard. The term is not defined in the Topic 6 deck: it comes from Examples PDF, Exercise 3 (extension).
subquestions.checkpoint_html:
• Four measurable indicators, each with its unit or ratio, linked to the objectives of the case: punctuality, data on time, spare parts, customer, adoption.
  • The link with controlling: standard, measurement, deviation, corrective action.
subquestions.solution_html:
Definition and link with controlling

A KPI is a quantified measure of performance against an objective (Examples PDF, Exercise 3; extension). It serves the second activity of controlling, measuring actual performance, so that deviations from the standard can be identified and corrected (Topic 6, Slide 24).

Four KPIs for Altair MRO

  1. On-time release rate: percentage of aircraft returned to the airline on or before the promised date (the problem that started the decision).
  2. Digital adoption rate: percentage of maintenance tasks recorded on the tablet instead of on paper, per hangar and per month.
  3. Spare-part waits: number of tasks stopped per month because a spare part was missing, which the automatic stock update should reduce.
  4. Customer satisfaction score: the airlines' rating of the information they receive on the progress of their aircraft, after each maintenance visit.

Other valid KPIs: hours of training completed per technician, number of task cards lost (should fall to zero), average turnaround time per check.

subquestions.label: e
subquestions.prompt_html: Hardest and easiest configuration
subquestions.hint_html: Compare what the platform needs (tasks and procedures that change quickly, information shared across departments, decisions taken close to the aircraft) with the coordination, specialization, standardization and centralization of each of the five configurations.
subquestions.checkpoint_html:
• Hardest: machine bureaucracy, with its features (rules and formal procedures, routine specialized tasks, functional departmentalization, centralized decisions, many layers, low span of control) matched to the facts of the statement.
  • Easiest: adhocracy (low standardization and formalization, decentralization, matrix departmentalization, used for specific projects).
  • Functional, divisional or matrix arguments are also accepted when reasoned.
subquestions.solution_html:
Hardest: machine bureaucracy

The machine bureaucracy has a proliferation of rules and very formalized procedures, highly specialized routine tasks, functional departmentalization, centralized decision-making and many layers with a low span of control (Topic 6, Slide 16). Altair MRO already shows these features: procedures "written in detailed manuals", a firm "organized by functions" with a head each, "six hierarchical levels" and every change "approved by the technical director". Every manual must be rewritten, the functional departments must start sharing data they keep separate today, and each change climbs six levels before it is approved, so the platform is hardest to introduce there.

Easiest: adhocracy

The adhocracy (innovative organization) has low standardization and formalization, decentralization as the key to flexibility, matrix departmentalization and a mix of middle line, operating core and staff, and it is used as a complementary structure for specific projects (Topic 6, Slide 22). A cross-functional project team can test the platform, change it and decide on the spot, so the introduction is easiest there; Altair MRO can use such a team for the pilot in one hangar, as part (a) proposes.

The other configurations and alternative answers

The simple structure decides quickly by direct supervision but is meant for start-ups and very small firms, not for 600 employees (Topic 6, Slide 15); in a professional bureaucracy qualified professionals decide on their own work (Topic 6, Slide 18), and in a division organization each division is a bureaucracy that can try the platform on its own (Topic 6, Slide 20). An answer that names a functional structure (departmental silos) as the hardest and a matrix structure as the easiest is also valid if it is reasoned (Examples PDF, Exercise 3): functional departmentalization is a feature of the machine bureaucracy and matrix departmentalization of the adhocracy (Topic 6, Slides 16 and 22).

items.interpretation_html: The case uses the whole of Topic 6: the decision is innovative and strategic (Slides 5 and 7), it is taken through the eight-step process (Slide 6), carried out through the four managerial functions (Slides 3-4), checked with indicators that serve controlling (Slide 24), and its difficulty depends on the configuration of the firm (Slides 15-22). The present structure of Altair MRO is close to a machine bureaucracy, so the advice is to pilot the platform in an adhocracy-like project team before extending it to the three hangars.

items.title: Celeris reusable launcher against an expendable incumbent
items.source: Case written for the bank in the style of Exercises 2 and 3 of BUSINESS_SECONDPARTIAL_2026_EXAMPLES_SOL.pdf (the examples PDF has no Topic 7 exercise); companies and figures are fictitious; not an official exercise. Content from Topic 7, Slides 3-19.
items.vault_note: vault/05 - Business Management/Problem Bank/Problem - Bank M05 - Celeris Reusable Launcher Against an Expendable Incumbent.md
items.statement_html:
Celeris Launch is a Spanish start-up founded in 2021 by four engineers who had worked for six years on the guidance of vertically landing vehicles in a university research group. The university's technology transfer office helped them license the guidance software and set up the company, and a private non-profit foundation, which does no research of its own, funded the last two years of the group's landing experiments. Celeris has its plant in an aerospace park where some twenty firms (structures, avionics, test services) share suppliers and customers; several of its engineers came from those neighbouring firms, bringing with them what they had learnt there. The national space agency granted Celeris access to the engine test stand of a government laboratory.

Celeris's small launcher has a reusable first stage: after separation it restarts its engines, deploys grid fins and landing legs, and lands vertically on a barge, so the stage, its engines and its guidance work together in a way no expendable launcher needs. The firm also 3D-prints the injector of its engine as a single piece instead of machining and brazing forty parts; the injector keeps the same geometry and performance, its production time falls from six weeks to five days, and the printers were already used in the plant for brackets. Finally, Carbotec, a composites supplier of the park, co-developed with Celeris a carbon-fibre interstage that replaces the aluminium one with the same shape and the same interfaces, and is 30% lighter.

The incumbent, Vektor Space, has built expendable launchers in series for thirty years; its strength is producing single-use stages cheaply, and it has no experience in landing guidance or in refurbishing a stage between flights. Its last three upgrades each cost more than the previous one and raised the payload delivered to orbit per million euros by less than 2%. Celeris's first flights delivered less payload per million euros than Vektor's launcher, but the figure has improved quickly with each landing and reuse. Celeris's chief executive says that "our design will become the standard of the industry as soon as the space agency declares it the official one".
items.setup_html:
Concept of the courseDefinition usedSource
